title: The log folder that filled up
story: A small log volume is mounted at /var/log/app. It is full, so the app cannot write. A background process called app-writer must keep running and keep writing heartbeat.log.
goals: Free the log volume so it is under 50 percent full.
Keep app-writer running.
Keep heartbeat.log and leave the volume mounted.
hints: Run df -h to see which volume is full.
Run ls -lh /var/log/app and see which files are large.
You may delete or empty the big log. Emptying with : > file keeps the file in place.
solution:
ls -lh /var/log/app
rm /var/log/app/debug.trace
: > /var/log/app/app.log
df -h /var/log/app

why.q: Why was emptying app.log with : > better than deleting it?
o: Deleting always frees nothing on Linux
: > asks the kernel to repair the disk
The writing process keeps its open file, so the file stays in place and its space is freed
why.x: A process holds the file open. Emptying it keeps the same file and frees the blocks now; deleting a file that is still open frees nothing until the process closes it.

title: Full disk with nothing to delete
story: The volume at /var/data is almost full, but ls shows no big file. A process called ingest deleted its queue file while still holding it open, so the space is not returned.
goals: Get /var/data under 60 percent full.
Keep the ingest process running (restart it if you must).
hints: du -sh /var/data shows little, but df -h shows it is full. Why would they differ?
A deleted file stays on disk while a process keeps it open. Look in /proc/PID/fd.
Run ls -l /proc/*/fd 2>/dev/null | grep deleted.
You can truncate through the descriptor, or stop the process and start it again.
solution:
ps | grep ingest
ls -l /proc/<pid>/fd | grep deleted
: > /proc/<pid>/fd/3
# or: kill <pid> and run /usr/local/bin/ingest again
df -h /var/data

why.q: Why did deleting the file not free any space?
o: The delete command is only a request and runs later
The process still had it open, so the data stayed until it was closed
The disk was too slow to update
why.x: A file's blocks are freed when the last name and the last open handle are gone. /proc/PID/fd shows the open handle, and truncating through it frees the space.

title: The deploy user cannot run the release script
story: The user deploy must run /srv/app/run.sh, but it fails. The directory and the file are both owned by root.
goals: Let the deploy user run /srv/app/run.sh.
Do not make the file or the folder writable by everyone.
hints: Try it: su -s /bin/sh deploy -c /srv/app/run.sh
ls -ld /srv/app and ls -l /srv/app/run.sh show owner, group and mode.
A user needs execute on the directory to enter it, and execute plus read on a script to run it.
solution:
chmod 755 /srv/app
chmod 755 /srv/app/run.sh
su -s /bin/sh deploy -c /srv/app/run.sh

why.q: The script was mode 755. Why did the deploy user still fail?
o: A parent folder also needs the execute bit to be entered
The user needs the script in its home folder
why.x: To use a path, every folder in it needs the x permission for you. A readable file inside a closed folder is still out of reach.

title: The job that eats the CPU
story: The machine feels slow. A runaway job started by report-job is burning CPU. A server called api-server must stay up.
goals: Stop report-job and everything it started.
Keep api-server running.
hints: Run top or ps to see the busy process.
Killing the busy process may not help if its parent starts it again.
Find the parent script, stop it first, then stop the child.
solution:
ps
kill $(pidof report-job)   # the parent loop first
kill $(pidof yes)
ps

why.q: Why kill the parent loop before the yes process?
o: Otherwise the loop starts a new yes straight away
The parent is the only one that can be stopped
why.x: A parent that restarts its child brings the hog back. Stopping the parent first means the child cannot be replaced.

title: The web server that will not start
story: start-web refuses to start the site. The settings file is /etc/web/web.conf and the site should answer on port 8080.
goals: Fix /etc/web/web.conf so PORT is 8080 and ROOT points to the real folder.
Start the server so http://127.0.0.1:8080/ answers.
hints: Run start-web and read the error message.
Compare PORT with a number: can you spot a letter?
ls /srv shows which folder really exists.
solution:
cat /etc/web/web.conf
sed -i "s/^PORT=.*/PORT=8080/;s#^ROOT=.*#ROOT=/srv/www#" /etc/web/web.conf
start-web
wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/

why.q: What is the fastest way to find why a service will not start?
o: Run its start command and read the error it prints
Delete the config and recreate it
why.x: The program says what it dislikes: a wrong port, a missing folder. The first error message nearly always names the setting to fix.

title: Port 8080 is taken
story: The new site must listen on port 8080, but an old web server still holds it. start-web starts the new one.
goals: Find and stop whatever holds port 8080.
Start the new site with start-web so port 8080 serves "MARGA web v2".
hints: netstat -tln lists the ports that are listening. Is 8080 one of them?
ps shows every process with its command line. Look for the one started with port 8080.
Stop that process, then run start-web.
solution:
netstat -tln | grep 8080
ps | grep httpd
kill <pid>
start-web
wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/

why.q: Why can two programs not listen on the same port?
o: A port belongs to one listening socket at a time
The network card allows one program only
Ports are reserved for the system
why.x: The kernel ties a listening port to one socket. The second program gets "address in use" until the first one stops or uses another port.

title: The pidfile that lies
story: start-web says the server is already running, but nothing answers on port 8080.
goals: Find out whether the process in the pidfile is really alive.
Start the server so it answers on port 8080 and leaves a valid pidfile.
hints: cat /run/web.pid shows the pid it remembers.
ls /proc/4242 or ps tells you if that pid is alive.
A pidfile for a dead process is stale and safe to remove.
solution:
cat /run/web.pid
ps | grep 4242
rm /run/web.pid
start-web
wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/

why.q: Why did start-web say it was running when it was not?
o: It only checks that the pidfile exists, not that the process lives
The process was hidden from ps
why.x: A crash leaves the pidfile behind. A careful script checks that the PID exists, for example with kill -0, before trusting the file.

title: The host name that does not resolve
story: The tool db-check must find the address of db.internal. Name lookups use /etc/hosts here. The database is reachable at 127.0.0.2 in this lab.
goals: Make db-check report db.internal as 127.0.0.2.
Keep the localhost entry in /etc/hosts.
hints: Run db-check and read the message.
cat /etc/hosts shows what names are known. Compare the spelling with db.internal.
Add a line: address, then the name.
solution:
cat /etc/hosts
echo "127.0.0.2 db.internal" >> /etc/hosts
db-check

why.q: What does /etc/hosts do?
o: It lists the files on the disk
It maps names to addresses before DNS is asked
why.x: The resolver reads /etc/hosts first on most systems, so a line there answers the name without DNS.

title: The release that points nowhere
story: /opt/app/current is a symlink to the active release, and it is broken. The newest release folder is under /opt/app/releases.
goals: Point /opt/app/current to the 2024-09 release.
Keep current as a symlink.
hints: ls -l /opt/app shows where current points.
ls /opt/app/releases shows which releases exist.
ln -sfn replaces a symlink in one step.
solution:
ls -l /opt/app
ls /opt/app/releases
ln -sfn releases/2024-09 /opt/app/current
app-status

why.q: What was wrong with the current link?
o: It pointed to a path that does not exist
why.x: A symbolic link just holds a path. If the target is missing, the link is broken, and ln -sfn repoints it.

title: Who is causing the 502 errors?
story: /var/log/web/access.log is a web access log. Field 1 is the client address and field 9 is the status code. Find how many 502 responses there are and which client has the most.
goals: Write two lines to /root/answer.txt: count=NUMBER and ip=ADDRESS.
count is the number of lines with status 502. ip is the client with the most 502 lines.
hints: head -3 /var/log/web/access.log shows the fields.
awk '$9==502' keeps only the 502 lines.
Count with wc -l. For the busiest client use awk, sort, uniq -c and sort -rn.
solution:
awk '$9==502' /var/log/web/access.log | wc -l
awk '$9==502{print $1}' /var/log/web/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1
printf 'count=N\nip=ADDRESS\n' > /root/answer.txt

why.q: Why count with sort, uniq -c and sort -rn?
o: It deletes duplicates from the file
It counts each address and puts the largest count first
It sorts the file on disk
why.x: uniq -c counts adjacent equal lines, so sort comes first to group them. sort -rn then puts the biggest count at the top.

title: The backup script that lies
story: /usr/local/bin/backup.sh copies a folder to /backup. It breaks on folder names with a space, and it prints "backup finished OK" even when the source is missing.
goals: backup.sh "/srv/my data" must copy the folder and exit 0.
backup.sh /srv/missing must exit non-zero and must not print "finished OK".
hints: Quote your variables: "$SRC".
Stop on errors: set -e, or check the result of cp.
Print the success message only after cp has worked.
solution:
cat > /usr/local/bin/backup.sh <<'X'
#!/bin/sh
set -eu
SRC=$1
cp -r "$SRC" /backup/
echo "backup finished OK"
X

why.q: What does set -e change in a script?
o: The script stops at the first failing command
It makes the script run faster
why.x: Without set -e a failing command is ignored and the script goes on to print success. With it the failure ends the script with an error.

title: The tool a new shell cannot find
story: The command deploytool lives in /opt/tools/bin and needs APP_ENV=staging. A new login shell must be able to run it with no extra typing.
goals: Make `sh -lc deploytool` work.
Do it in a startup file, not by copying the tool.
hints: A login shell reads /etc/profile and then ~/.profile.
Put an export PATH line and an export APP_ENV line in /root/.profile.
Test with a new login shell: sh -lc deploytool
solution:
cat >> /root/.profile <<'X'
export PATH=$PATH:/opt/tools/bin
export APP_ENV=staging
X
sh -lc deploytool

why.q: Why was the tool not found in a new shell?
o: PATH was set only in the old session, not in a start-up file
why.x: Variables belong to the shell that set them. A file like .profile is read by each new login shell, so put exports there.

title: The setting in the hidden file
story: The app in /srv/app runs in debug mode in production. Its settings live in a hidden file, so a plain ls shows nothing useful.
goals: Set DEBUG=false in the hidden settings file of /srv/app.
Keep every other setting in that file.
hints: Hidden files start with a dot. ls -a shows them.
The file is /srv/app/.env. Open it with cat to see the settings.
sed -i can change one line in place: sed -i "s/old/new/" file.
solution:
ls -a /srv/app
cat /srv/app/.env
sed -i "s/^DEBUG=true/DEBUG=false/" /srv/app/.env
cat /srv/app/.env

why.q: Why did ls not show the .env file?
o: Names that start with a dot are hidden unless you use -a
why.x: ls hides dotfiles by default. ls -a shows them, and many tools keep settings in them.

title: Where did the invoice go?
story: Finance saved invoice-2026-0417.pdf somewhere under /srv/archive, in one of many folders. You need a copy in /root.
goals: Find invoice-2026-0417.pdf under /srv/archive.
Copy it to /root/invoice.pdf.
Leave the original where it is.
hints: find searches a folder tree by name: find /srv/archive -name "pattern".
Quote the pattern so the shell does not expand it first.
cp SOURCE DEST copies a file. You can put find inside $( ) to use its result.
solution:
find /srv/archive -name "invoice-2026-0417.pdf"
cp "$(find /srv/archive -name invoice-2026-0417.pdf)" /root/invoice.pdf

why.q: Why is find better than looking folder by folder?
o: It is faster because it only reads file names in the top folder
It searches a whole tree by name, size or date
why.x: find walks the tree for you and filters by many properties, so you do not have to guess the folder.

title: Permission denied on the report script
story: The command hello-report was copied to the server, but running it says permission denied. It should print "report ready".
goals: Make hello-report run when you type its name.
Do not rewrite the script.
hints: ls -l shows the permission bits. An x means executable.
The file is /usr/local/bin/hello-report.
chmod +x FILE adds the executable bit.
solution:
ls -l /usr/local/bin/hello-report
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/hello-report
hello-report

why.q: What does chmod +x do?
o: It copies the file to the PATH
It sets the execute permission so the file can be run
why.x: A file needs the x bit to be run directly. Without it, the shell answers Permission denied even if you can read the file.

title: The script that points at a missing shell
story: cleanup.sh was written on a laptop and starts with #!/bin/bash. This small server only has /bin/sh, so the script cannot start.
goals: Make /opt/tools/cleanup.sh run and print "cleanup done".
Change only what is needed.
hints: Run /opt/tools/cleanup.sh and read the error. It names the interpreter it cannot find.
The first line of a script says which program runs it.
Change line 1 to #!/bin/sh. sed -i "1s|.*|NEWLINE|" file replaces line 1.
solution:
/opt/tools/cleanup.sh
head -1 /opt/tools/cleanup.sh
sed -i "1s|.*|#!/bin/sh|" /opt/tools/cleanup.sh
/opt/tools/cleanup.sh

why.q: What does the first line #!/bin/bash do?
o: It names the program that runs the script
It is just a comment with no effect
why.x: The kernel reads #! and starts that program with the script. If the program is missing, you get a confusing "not found" error.

title: The script with Windows line endings
story: sync.sh was edited on Windows. It fails with a strange "not found" error even though the file is there.
goals: Make /opt/tools/sync.sh run and print "sync ok".
Remove the Windows line endings. Do not retype the script.
hints: cat -A style tools show hidden characters. Try: od -c /opt/tools/sync.sh | head.
Windows ends each line with CR LF. Linux expects only LF. The extra CR sticks to the interpreter name.
sed -i "s/\r$//" file removes the CR. dos2unix file does the same.
solution:
od -c /opt/tools/sync.sh | head -3
sed -i "s/\r$//" /opt/tools/sync.sh
/opt/tools/sync.sh

why.q: Why did Windows line endings break the script?
o: The hidden carriage return became part of each command
why.x: A CR character stays at the end of every line, so the shell looks for a command named with a stray \r. sed removes it.

title: The upload folder the app cannot write to
story: The web app runs as the user webapp. Uploads fail with "permission denied" because /srv/uploads belongs to root.
goals: Let the user webapp create files in /srv/uploads.
Do not make the folder writable by everyone.
hints: ls -ld /srv/uploads shows the owner and the mode.
Only the owner or root can write to a mode 755 folder.
chown webapp /srv/uploads gives the folder to that user.
solution:
ls -ld /srv/uploads
chown webapp /srv/uploads
ls -ld /srv/uploads

why.q: Why could the app not write to the folder?
o: The folder belonged to another user and gave others no write access
why.x: Writing needs the w permission for the user that runs the process. chown gives the folder to the right owner.

title: Maya cannot open the reports
story: The analysts group owns /srv/reports. Maya joined the team but cannot read q3.txt. Mode 777 would "work" but is not allowed.
goals: Let the user maya read /srv/reports/q3.txt.
Do it with group membership, not with open permissions.
hints: ls -ld /srv/reports and id maya show the folder group and her groups.
Group members are listed in /etc/group, in the last field of the group line.
Add maya to the analysts line: sed -i "s/^analysts:\(.*\):$/analysts:\1:maya/" /etc/group, or edit the line with vi.
solution:
ls -ld /srv/reports
grep analysts /etc/group
sed -i "s/^analysts:x:2000:$/analysts:x:2000:maya/" /etc/group
id maya

why.q: Why did adding Maya to the group help?
o: The folder allowed the group, and group membership gives her that access
The group file is a backup
why.x: Permissions have owner, group and others parts. Joining the group moves Maya into the group part, which already allowed access.

title: Everyone can delete everyone else's files
story: /srv/share is open to all users, but people keep deleting each other's files. Users should only be able to delete their own.
goals: Keep the folder usable by everyone.
Set the sticky bit so only a file's owner can delete it.
hints: ls -ld /srv/share shows rwxrwxrwx. A sticky folder shows a t at the end.
The sticky bit is the leading 1 in a four-digit mode.
chmod 1777 /srv/share, or chmod +t /srv/share.
solution:
ls -ld /srv/share
chmod 1777 /srv/share
ls -ld /srv/share

why.q: What does the sticky bit on a shared folder do?
o: Only a file's owner can delete or rename it
why.x: With the sticky bit (like /tmp) everyone can create files, but only the owner of a file, or root, can remove it.

title: The process that ignores a polite stop
story: stuck-job ignores the normal stop signal and keeps running. web-heartbeat is healthy and must keep running.
goals: Stop stuck-job.
Leave web-heartbeat running.
hints: ps shows the running programs. pidof stuck-job prints its process id.
kill PID sends the polite signal TERM. This job ignores it.
kill -9 PID cannot be ignored. Use it when the polite stop fails.
solution:
ps | grep stuck
kill $(pidof stuck-job)
kill -9 $(pidof stuck-job)
ps | grep stuck

why.q: Why did kill alone not stop the process?
o: It ignores the polite signal, so you need kill -9
kill only works on root's processes
why.x: SIGTERM can be caught or ignored. SIGKILL (-9) cannot be caught, so it works when the program is stuck, but gives no chance to clean up.

title: Which folder is eating the disk?
story: Under /srv/data there are several folders. Someone asks which one is the biggest. Write its name into /root/answer.txt as biggest=NAME.
goals: Find the largest folder directly under /srv/data.
Write biggest=NAME (just the folder name) into /root/answer.txt.
hints: du -sk FOLDER prints the size in kilobytes.
du -sk /srv/data/* lists every folder with its size.
Sort the sizes with sort -rn and take the first line.
solution:
du -sk /srv/data/*
echo "biggest=$(du -sk /srv/data/* | sort -rn | head -1 | awk -F/ '{print $NF}')" > /root/answer.txt
cat /root/answer.txt

why.q: Why is du -sk with sort -rn useful?
o: It sizes each folder and shows the largest first
why.x: du adds up space per folder, and sort -rn puts the largest number at the top, so the culprit is easy to see.

title: Back up the site before the change
story: Before a risky change, make a compressed backup of the website in /srv/site. Put it at /backup/site.tar.gz.
goals: Create /backup/site.tar.gz holding everything in /srv/site.
Leave /srv/site as it is.
hints: tar c creates an archive, z compresses it with gzip, f names the file.
tar czf ARCHIVE FOLDER. Use -C DIR to stay out of absolute paths.
Check the result with tar tzf /backup/site.tar.gz.
solution:
mkdir -p /backup
tar czf /backup/site.tar.gz -C /srv site
tar tzf /backup/site.tar.gz

why.q: Why use tar czf for a backup?
o: It bundles many files into one compressed archive
why.x: tar packs files and folders into one file, and z compresses it. One file is easy to store, move and test.

title: Unpack the release
story: A release archive is in /root. Unpack it into /opt/app so that /opt/app/bin/run works and /opt/app/VERSION says 1.4.
goals: Extract /root/release-1.4.tar.gz into /opt/app.
Running /opt/app/bin/run should print "run 1.4".
hints: tar tzf ARCHIVE lists what is inside without extracting.
tar xzf ARCHIVE extracts. -C DIR picks the target folder, which must exist.
mkdir -p /opt/app first, then tar xzf /root/release-1.4.tar.gz -C /opt/app.
solution:
tar tzf /root/release-1.4.tar.gz
mkdir -p /opt/app
tar xzf /root/release-1.4.tar.gz -C /opt/app
/opt/app/bin/run

why.q: What does tar tzf let you do before extracting?
why.x: Looking first shows where the files will land, so you do not scatter files into the current folder.

title: How many errors today?
story: The app log mixes INFO, WARN and ERROR lines. Some INFO lines mention the word "error" in lower case. Count only the lines whose level is ERROR and save the number in /root/errors.txt.
goals: Count the lines at level ERROR in /var/log/app/app.log.
Write only the number into /root/errors.txt.
hints: grep prints matching lines. grep -c prints how many match.
The level sits between spaces: " ERROR ". Searching for the level avoids the lower-case words.
grep -c " ERROR " /var/log/app/app.log > /root/errors.txt
solution:
grep -c " ERROR " /var/log/app/app.log
grep -c " ERROR " /var/log/app/app.log > /root/errors.txt

why.q: Why use grep -c?
o: It searches only the first line
It counts matching lines instead of printing them
why.x: -c prints the number of lines that match, which is exactly what a report needs.

title: How many different visitors?
story: /srv/data/visitors.txt has one visitor name per line, with many repeats. Count the different names and save the number in /root/unique.txt.
goals: Count unique names in /srv/data/visitors.txt.
Write only the number into /root/unique.txt.
hints: sort puts equal lines next to each other. sort -u removes repeats.
wc -l counts lines.
sort -u FILE | wc -l > /root/unique.txt
solution:
sort -u /srv/data/visitors.txt | wc -l
sort -u /srv/data/visitors.txt | wc -l > /root/unique.txt

why.q: Why does sort -u then wc -l count distinct values?
o: sort -u removes repeated lines and wc -l counts what is left
why.x: sort -u keeps one copy of each line. Counting the remaining lines gives the number of different visitors.

title: Name the server
story: This server still calls itself localhost. It should be called web-01, in /etc/hostname and in the 127.0.1.1 line of /etc/hosts. Keep the localhost line.
goals: Put web-01 in /etc/hostname.
Make the 127.0.1.1 line of /etc/hosts say web-01.
Keep the 127.0.0.1 localhost line.
hints: cat /etc/hostname and cat /etc/hosts show the current names.
echo web-01 > /etc/hostname replaces the file.
sed -i "s/^127.0.1.1.*/127.0.1.1 web-01/" /etc/hosts changes one line.
solution:
echo web-01 > /etc/hostname
sed -i "s/^127.0.1.1.*/127.0.1.1 web-01/" /etc/hosts
cat /etc/hostname /etc/hosts

why.q: Why can the hostname show in more than one place?
o: Every file has its own name
A machine's name is kept in /etc/hostname and often repeated in /etc/hosts
The name is stored in the BIOS only
why.x: The system reads /etc/hostname at boot, and /etc/hosts lets the name resolve locally. They should agree.

title: The machine cannot talk to itself
story: Local services cannot reach each other: even ping 127.0.0.1 fails. The web service on port 8080 is running, but nothing can connect to it.
goals: Make ping 127.0.0.1 work again.
Make http://127.0.0.1:8080/ answer.
hints: ifconfig -a lists all interfaces, even down ones. A working one shows UP.
The loopback interface is called lo.
ifconfig lo up (or ifconfig lo 127.0.0.1 up) brings it back.
solution:
ping -c 1 127.0.0.1
ifconfig -a
ifconfig lo 127.0.0.1 up
ping -c 1 127.0.0.1

why.q: What did the loopback interface need?
o: It had to be brought up with an address
why.x: lo is a virtual interface. If it is down, even connections from the machine to itself fail.

title: The health check looks at the wrong port
story: The web service runs on port 8080 and is fine. The health check says "unhealthy" because its settings point at another port. Fix the check, not the service.
goals: Make the command healthcheck print "healthy".
Keep the web service on port 8080.
hints: Run healthcheck and read what it says. cat /usr/local/bin/healthcheck shows where it reads its settings.
The settings file is /etc/monitor.conf.
sed -i "s/8081/8080/" /etc/monitor.conf
solution:
healthcheck
cat /etc/monitor.conf
sed -i "s/8081/8080/" /etc/monitor.conf
healthcheck

why.q: Why does a health check fail when the service is fine?
o: The check looks at a port the service does not use
why.x: A check is only as right as its config. Compare the port in the check with the port the service listens on (netstat -tln).

title: Rename every .txt to .md
story: The docs in /srv/docs are plain text but the new site generator wants Markdown. Rename every .txt file to .md. Do not touch the .log file.
goals: No .txt files remain in /srv/docs.
Each file keeps its text, now with the .md ending.
notes.log is left alone.
hints: ls /srv/docs shows the files.
A loop can do many: for f in /srv/docs/*.txt; do ...; done
${f%.txt} removes the ending: mv "$f" "${f%.txt}.md"
solution:
ls /srv/docs
for f in /srv/docs/*.txt; do mv "$f" "${f%.txt}.md"; done
ls /srv/docs

why.q: What does ${f%.txt} do in the loop?
o: It removes .txt from the end of the name
why.x: ${var%suffix} trims the shortest matching suffix, so you can build the new name with .md.

title: Send the data one way and the warnings another
story: The command noisy prints data lines to standard output and warnings to standard error. Run it once so the data lands in /root/out.log and the warnings in /root/err.log.
goals: /root/out.log holds only the data lines.
/root/err.log holds only the warning lines.
hints: Run noisy and watch the screen: both kinds of lines appear.
> sends standard output to a file. 2> sends standard error.
noisy > /root/out.log 2> /root/err.log
solution:
noisy
noisy > /root/out.log 2> /root/err.log
cat /root/out.log /root/err.log

why.q: What are stdout and stderr?
o: Two copies of the same output
Two output streams: normal data and warnings or errors
why.x: Programs write results to stdout and problems to stderr. > redirects the first, 2> the second.

title: Clear out the old cache files
story: /var/cache/app holds cache files of different ages. Delete the ones older than 7 days and keep the newer ones.
goals: Delete every cache file older than 7 days.
Keep the files that are 7 days old or newer.
hints: ls -l shows dates. find can test the age of files.
find DIR -type f -mtime +7 lists files older than 7 days.
Add -exec rm {} \; to delete what find lists. List first, then delete.
solution:
ls -l /var/cache/app
find /var/cache/app -type f -mtime +7
find /var/cache/app -type f -mtime +7 -exec rm {} \;
ls -l /var/cache/app

why.q: What does find -mtime +7 match?
o: Files modified more than 7 days ago
why.x: -mtime counts days since the last change. +7 means older than 7 days, a safe way to clear a cache.

title: The volume that turned read-only
story: /srv/records is mounted read-only, so the app cannot save anything. The data on it must stay.
goals: Make /srv/records writable again.
Keep the existing ledger file and keep the volume mounted.
hints: touch /srv/records/x tells you the error. mount | grep records shows the options, and ro means read-only.
You do not need to unmount. A remount changes the options in place.
mount -o remount,rw /srv/records
solution:
mount | grep records
mount -o remount,rw /srv/records
touch /srv/records/test && echo writable

why.q: How was the volume made writable again?
why.x: After disk errors the kernel can remount read-only. mount -o remount,rw changes the mode, but check the cause first.

title: Copy the file with a space in its name
story: Two quarterly reports are in /srv/papers. One of them has a space in its name. Copy "Q3 report.txt" to /backup without renaming it.
goals: /backup/Q3 report.txt exists with the same content.
The original stays in /srv/papers.
hints: Try cp /srv/papers/Q3 report.txt /backup and read the error. The shell sees two names.
Quotes keep a name with spaces together: "Q3 report.txt".
cp "/srv/papers/Q3 report.txt" /backup/
solution:
ls /srv/papers
cp "/srv/papers/Q3 report.txt" /backup/
ls /backup

why.q: Why quote a name that has a space?
o: Without quotes the shell sees two separate words
why.x: The shell splits on spaces. Quotes keep "Q3 report.txt" as one argument.

title: The backup runs hourly, not every five minutes
story: The crontab for root runs /usr/local/bin/backup once an hour. It should run every 5 minutes.
goals: The root crontab runs /usr/local/bin/backup every 5 minutes.
It has one backup line, not two.
hints: crontab -l shows the table. The five fields are minute, hour, day, month, weekday.
*/5 in the minute field means every 5 minutes.
echo "*/5 * * * * /usr/local/bin/backup" | crontab -  replaces the table.
solution:
crontab -l
echo "*/5 * * * * /usr/local/bin/backup" | crontab -
crontab -l

why.q: Which cron schedule means every five minutes?
why.x: The first field is minutes. */5 means every fifth minute; 5 alone means minute 5 of every hour.

title: Linux paths are case sensitive
story: The command app-info should print the app name from the app's config file. It prints nothing useful because the path in the script uses the wrong case.
goals: Make app-info print "name: shop".
Fix the path in the script. Do not rename the folder.
hints: Run app-info, then ls /srv to see the real folder name.
/srv/App and /srv/app are different folders on Linux.
sed -i "s#/srv/App#/srv/app#" /usr/local/bin/app-info
solution:
app-info
ls /srv
sed -i "s#/srv/App#/srv/app#" /usr/local/bin/app-info
app-info

why.q: Why did /srv/App fail when /srv/app exists?
o: Linux file names are case sensitive
why.x: Linux treats App and app as different names, unlike some other systems.

title: Rotate the log without stopping the app
story: app.log has grown big. Rotate it by hand: keep the old lines compressed as app.log.1.gz and let the app go on writing a fresh app.log. The logger process must keep running.
goals: /var/log/svc/app.log.1.gz holds the old lines.
A new /var/log/svc/app.log exists and is being written.
app-logger keeps running.
hints: ls -l /var/log/svc shows the size. The logger opens the file by path each time it writes.
Move the file away first, then compress the moved copy.
mv app.log app.log.1, then gzip app.log.1. The logger creates a new app.log by itself.
solution:
cd /var/log/svc
mv app.log app.log.1
gzip app.log.1
sleep 2; ls -l

why.q: Why is it safe to rename a log that an app writes to?
o: The app keeps writing into the same open file, now under its new name
why.x: A process holds the file, not the name. After the rename it still writes to the same file; that is why apps need a reopen signal later.

title: Works in my shell, fails in cron
story: nightly.sh runs fine when you type it, but cron runs jobs with a tiny PATH, and the tool it calls lives in /opt/tools/bin. The job fails at night.
goals: Make /opt/job/nightly.sh work with a minimal PATH (only /usr/bin and /bin).
It should print "nightly ok".
hints: Test like cron: env -i PATH=/usr/bin:/bin /opt/job/nightly.sh
The script calls mytool by name. cron cannot find it. Where is it? find /opt -name mytool
Call it by its full path in the script, or set PATH at the top of the script.
solution:
env -i PATH=/usr/bin:/bin /opt/job/nightly.sh
find /opt -name mytool
sed -i "s#^mytool#/opt/tools/bin/mytool#" /opt/job/nightly.sh
env -i PATH=/usr/bin:/bin /opt/job/nightly.sh

why.q: Why did the job work in the shell but not in cron?
o: Cron runs with a tiny environment and a short PATH
why.x: Cron does not read your profile. Use full paths in the job, or set PATH in the script.

title: Two lines for the same name
story: /etc/hosts has two entries for api.internal. The first one is an old address, and the first match wins. api-check keeps failing.
goals: Make api-check print "api ok".
Keep the localhost line.
hints: Run api-check and cat /etc/hosts. Look for the name appearing twice.
Resolvers use the first matching line. The old address 10.1.1.5 is unreachable.
Delete the stale line: sed -i "/^10.1.1.5 /d" /etc/hosts
solution:
api-check
grep api.internal /etc/hosts
sed -i "/^10.1.1.5 /d" /etc/hosts
api-check

why.q: Why did the old address win?
o: The first matching line in /etc/hosts is used
why.x: The resolver stops at the first match, so an old line above a new one hides the right address.

title: The app starts before its database
story: stack-up starts the services listed in /etc/stack.order, in that order. The app refuses to start unless the database is ready, but the list has them the wrong way round.
goals: Run stack-up so that both db-svc and app-svc are running.
Fix the order file, do not edit the service scripts.
hints: Run stack-up and read the error. cat /etc/stack.order shows the order.
Each line is a service name. The database must come first.
printf "db\napp\n" > /etc/stack.order, then run stack-up again.
solution:
stack-up
cat /etc/stack.order
printf "db\napp\n" > /etc/stack.order
stack-up

why.q: Why does the order of starting matter?
o: The app needs the database to be ready first
why.x: Dependencies must be up before what needs them. A start order file or a unit dependency expresses that.

title: The settings file with spaces around the equals sign
story: run-app loads /etc/app/app.env as shell code. The file was written like an INI file with spaces around "=", and the shell tries to run the names as commands.
goals: Make run-app print "connecting to db1:5432".
Keep both settings.
hints: Run run-app and read the errors: "DB_HOST: not found".
In shell, VAR=value must have no spaces around the equals sign.
sed -i "s/ = /=/" /etc/app/app.env
solution:
run-app
cat /etc/app/app.env
sed -i "s/ = /=/" /etc/app/app.env
run-app

why.q: Why do spaces around = break an env file?
o: Shell assignments need NAME=value with no spaces
Spaces are only allowed in names
why.x: In a shell, NAME = value runs a command called NAME. The setting must be written NAME=value.

title: The service is running as root
story: webd must never run as root, but someone started it from a root shell. Run it as the user webapp instead and leave no root copy running.
goals: Exactly one webd process runs.
It runs as the user webapp.
hints: ps -o user,comm shows which user owns each process.
Stop the root copy with kill, then start a new one as the right user.
su -s /bin/sh webapp -c "/usr/local/bin/webd >/dev/null 2>&1 &"
solution:
ps -o user,comm | grep webd
kill $(pidof webd)
su -s /bin/sh webapp -c "/usr/local/bin/webd >/dev/null 2>&1 &"
ps -o user,comm | grep webd

why.q: Why not run a web service as root?
o: If it is hacked, the attacker gets root
why.x: Least privilege: a service account limits the damage of a break-in to what that user can reach.

title: Slow down the batch job without killing it
story: batch-crunch is useful, so it must finish, but it is hogging the CPU at normal priority and slowing the API. Give it a low priority (nice 10 or more). api-server must stay untouched.
goals: batch-crunch keeps running with nice 10 or higher.
api-server keeps running at its normal priority.
hints: top (press q to quit) or ps shows what is busy.
The nice value runs from -20 (greedy) to 19 (polite). renice changes it for a running process.
renice -n 15 -p PID or renice 15 -p PID. Get the PID with pidof batch-crunch.
solution:
pidof batch-crunch
renice 15 -p $(pidof batch-crunch)
ps -o pid,nice,comm | grep -E "batch|api"

why.q: What does renice do?
o: It changes how much CPU time a process gets compared with others
why.x: A higher nice value means lower priority. The job keeps running but yields to important work.

title: Staging works, production does not
story: The same app behaves differently in staging and production. The two config files should be identical except for one line. Find the key that differs and write it as key=NAME in /root/answer.txt.
goals: Compare /root/staging.conf and /root/prod.conf.
Write the name of the one key whose value differs into /root/answer.txt as key=NAME.
hints: diff FILE1 FILE2 shows the lines that differ. Busybox diff prints a unified diff: lines starting with - come from the first file and + from the second.
The key is the part before the equals sign.
echo "key=$(diff /root/staging.conf /root/prod.conf | sed -n "s/^-\([A-Z_]*\)=.*/\1/p")" > /root/answer.txt
solution:
diff /root/staging.conf /root/prod.conf
echo "key=$(diff /root/staging.conf /root/prod.conf | sed -n 's/^-\([A-Z_]*\)=.*/\1/p')" > /root/answer.txt
cat /root/answer.txt

why.q: What is a quick way to find the difference between two files?
o: diff shows the lines that differ
why.x: diff prints exactly the lines that are not the same, so a single changed key stands out.

title: Change a setting in one section only
story: app.ini has a port setting in each of three sections. Only the [db] port must change, from 5432 to 5433. The other ports must stay as they are.
goals: The port under [db] is 5433.
The ports under [cache] and [web] are unchanged.
hints: cat /etc/app/app.ini shows three "port=" lines. A plain sed on "port=" would change all of them.
sed can limit a change to a range of lines: sed "/start/,/end/ s/a/b/".
sed -i "/^\[db\]/,/^\[cache\]/ s/^port=5432/port=5433/" /etc/app/app.ini
solution:
cat /etc/app/app.ini
sed -i "/^\[db\]/,/^\[cache\]/ s/^port=5432/port=5433/" /etc/app/app.ini
cat /etc/app/app.ini

why.q: Why restrict the sed edit to a range?
o: The same key exists in several sections
why.x: A sed address like /^\[db\]/,/^\[cache\]/ limits the edit, so port in [cache] stays untouched.

title: How much data did the good requests send?
story: In the access log, the status code is in the 9th field and the response size in the 10th. Add up the sizes of all requests that returned 200 and save it as bytes=NUMBER in /root/answer.txt.
goals: Sum the bytes of the 200 responses in /var/log/web/access.log.
Write bytes=NUMBER into /root/answer.txt.
hints: head -3 /var/log/web/access.log shows the line format. awk splits lines into fields $1, $2, and so on.
awk can add: awk '$9==200 {s+=$10} END {print s}' FILE
echo "bytes=$(awk '$9==200{s+=$10} END{print s}' /var/log/web/access.log)" > /root/answer.txt
solution:
head -3 /var/log/web/access.log
echo "bytes=$(awk '$9==200{s+=$10} END{print s}' /var/log/web/access.log)" > /root/answer.txt
cat /root/answer.txt

why.q: What does awk '$9==200{s+=$10} END{print s}' do?
o: It adds up column 10 for lines whose status is 200
why.x: awk runs the action on lines that match the condition, adds the bytes, and prints the total at the end.

title: Delete the temp files, even the ones with spaces
story: /srv/work is full of *.tmp files, some with spaces in their names. Delete all of them. The .keep files must stay.
goals: No .tmp file remains under /srv/work.
Every .keep file is still there.
hints: find /srv/work -name "*.tmp" lists the files.
Names with spaces break a plain pipe into rm. find can run the command itself.
find /srv/work -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \;  or  find ... -print0 | xargs -0 rm
solution:
find /srv/work -name "*.tmp"
find /srv/work -name "*.tmp" -print0 | xargs -0 rm
find /srv/work -type f

why.q: Why use -print0 with xargs -0?
o: It separates names with a null character, so spaces are safe
why.x: A name can contain spaces or even newlines, but never a NUL byte. Using NUL as the separator keeps each name whole.

title: The site only the owner can read
story: The web server user www gets "permission denied" for everything under /srv/site, because the files were copied with private permissions. Folders should be 755 and files 644, and nothing may be writable by others.
goals: The user www can read /srv/site/css/app.css.
All folders under /srv/site are 755 and all files 644.
hints: ls -lR /srv/site shows modes everywhere. Folders need x so people can enter them.
find can pick only folders (-type d) or only files (-type f).
find /srv/site -type d -exec chmod 755 {} \;  and  find /srv/site -type f -exec chmod 644 {} \;

why.q: Why chmod folders and files differently?
o: Folders need x to be entered, files normally do not
why.x: 755 for folders lets people enter them; 644 for files lets them read without making data executable.

title: New files should belong to the team group
story: People in the devs group share /srv/proj. Files created there get the creator's own group, so teammates cannot edit them. New files should automatically get the group devs.
goals: A file created by the user alice in /srv/proj belongs to the group devs.
The folder stays group-writable for devs.
hints: ls -ld /srv/proj shows the group. New files normally get the creator's primary group.
The setgid bit on a folder makes new files inherit the folder's group.
chmod g+s /srv/proj  (or chmod 2775 /srv/proj)
solution:
ls -ld /srv/proj
chmod g+s /srv/proj
ls -ld /srv/proj

why.q: What does the setgid bit on a folder do?
o: New files get the folder's group
why.x: With g+s new files inherit the folder's group, so a team shares files without chgrp each time.

title: Disk has space but no new files
story: The session store /var/sessions cannot create new files: "No space left on device". But df -h shows plenty of free space. The old session files must go, and the current-session marker must stay.
goals: New files can be created in /var/sessions again.
The file current-session is kept and the volume stays mounted.
hints: df -h shows free space; df -i shows free inodes. Every file needs one inode.
Count the files: ls /var/sessions | wc -l
Remove the old session files: rm /var/sessions/sess-*
solution:
df -h /var/sessions
df -i /var/sessions
rm /var/sessions/sess-*
df -i /var/sessions

why.q: What does df -i show?
o: How many inodes (file slots) are used and free
why.x: A file system has a fixed number of inodes. A million tiny files can use them up while blocks remain free.

title: Two services, one port
story: service A and service B are both set to port 8080. A started first. B failed to start with an address-in-use error. Both must run: A on 8080 and B on 8081.
goals: http://127.0.0.1:8080/ answers "service A".
http://127.0.0.1:8081/ answers "service B".
hints: Only one program can listen on a port. Read what start-b printed. cat /etc/svc-b.conf shows its port.
Change the port in B's config, not A's.
sed -i "s/8080/8081/" /etc/svc-b.conf, then run start-b.
solution:
cat /etc/svc-a.conf /etc/svc-b.conf
sed -i "s/8080/8081/" /etc/svc-b.conf
start-b

why.q: Whose port should change when both want 8080?
o: The one that is easier or safer to move, here service B
why.x: Pick one clear owner for 8080, and move the other. Do not break a service that is already working.

title: 404 for a page that is there
story: The site on port 8085 returns "404 Not Found" for the home page, but the HTML file is in the folder. A web server looks for index.html in lower case.
goals: http://127.0.0.1:8085/ shows "Welcome to the shop".
Do not restart the server.
hints: wget -S -O - http://127.0.0.1:8085/ shows the status line. ls /srv/shop shows what is in the folder.
The file is called Index.html. On Linux, file names are case sensitive.
mv /srv/shop/Index.html /srv/shop/index.html
solution:
wget -S -O - http://127.0.0.1:8085/
ls /srv/shop
mv /srv/shop/Index.html /srv/shop/index.html
wget -q -O - http://127.0.0.1:8085/

why.q: Why did the web server answer 404?
o: It looks for index.html and the file is named Index.html
why.x: Names are case sensitive. The default index file is exactly index.html.

title: The service wants an address the machine does not have
story: The API must listen on 10.20.30.40, port 8090. start-api fails with a bind error because that address is not configured on this machine.
goals: Give the machine the address 10.20.30.40.
Start the API so http://10.20.30.40:8090/ answers "api ok".
hints: Run start-api and read the error. ip addr shows the addresses the machine has.
You can add an address to an interface: ip addr add ADDRESS/32 dev lo
ip addr add 10.20.30.40/32 dev lo, then start-api.
solution:
start-api
ip addr
ip addr add 10.20.30.40/32 dev lo
start-api

why.q: What does "cannot assign requested address" mean?
o: The service wants an address this machine does not have
why.x: A program can only bind to an address that belongs to one of the machine's interfaces. ip addr lists them.

title: The old tool wins
story: Two versions of deploytool are installed. The old 1.0 is in /usr/local/bin and the new 2.0 is in /opt/deploy/bin. After login, typing deploytool runs the old one, because the login profile appends the new folder at the end of PATH.
goals: After a login, deploytool prints "deploytool 2.0".
Keep the old version installed.
hints: which deploytool shows which one runs. PATH is searched from left to right.
/root/.profile adds /opt/deploy/bin at the end. It must come first.
echo 'export PATH=/opt/deploy/bin:$PATH' >> /root/.profile
solution:
which deploytool
cat /root/.profile
echo 'export PATH=/opt/deploy/bin:$PATH' >> /root/.profile
. /root/.profile; deploytool

why.q: Which directory in PATH wins?
o: The first one that contains the command
why.x: The shell searches PATH from left to right, so putting your directory first makes your tool win.

title: Listening only on the loopback address
story: The web service works from the machine itself (127.0.0.1) but not from the "outside" address 127.0.0.2. It was started bound to 127.0.0.1 only. Make it answer on every address.
goals: http://127.0.0.2:8095/ answers "public site".
http://127.0.0.1:8095/ still answers.
hints: wget http://127.0.0.1:8095/ works, wget http://127.0.0.2:8095/ does not. netstat -ltn shows the listening address.
The server was started with -p 127.0.0.1:8095. Without an address it listens on all of them.
kill $(pidof httpd); httpd -p 8095 -h /srv/public
solution:
netstat -ltn
kill $(pidof httpd)
httpd -p 8095 -h /srv/public
netstat -ltn

why.q: What does listening on 127.0.0.1 mean?
o: Only programs on the same machine can connect
why.x: 127.0.0.1 is loopback. 0.0.0.0 listens on all addresses, so other machines can reach it.

title: SSH ignores the key
story: The user deploy cannot log in with a key. The SSH server refuses key files that other people can read or write, or that belong to the wrong user. Fix the owner and the modes.
goals: /home/deploy/.ssh and authorized_keys belong to deploy.
.ssh is mode 700 and authorized_keys is mode 600.
hints: ls -ld /home/deploy/.ssh and ls -l /home/deploy/.ssh show owner and modes.
Three things are wrong: the owner, the folder mode and the file mode.
chown -R deploy:deploy /home/deploy/.ssh; chmod 700 /home/deploy/.ssh; chmod 600 /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys
solution:
ls -ld /home/deploy/.ssh
ls -l /home/deploy/.ssh
chown -R deploy:deploy /home/deploy/.ssh
chmod 700 /home/deploy/.ssh
chmod 600 /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys

why.q: Why does SSH ignore a key with loose permissions?
o: It refuses keys that others could read or change
why.x: SSH checks .ssh (700) and private keys (600). If others can touch them, they could be stolen, so it ignores them.

title: A service account that can log in
story: The account svc-backup only runs a nightly backup, but its entry in /etc/passwd gives it a normal login shell. Service accounts must not be able to log in. Do not change anything else about the account.
goals: The shell of svc-backup is /bin/false (or a nologin shell).
Its user id (997) and home folder stay the same.
root keeps /bin/sh.
hints: grep svc-backup /etc/passwd. The last field is the shell.
Fields are separated by colons. The shell is field 7.
sed -i 's|^\(svc-backup:.*:\)/bin/sh$|\1/bin/false|' /etc/passwd
solution:
grep svc-backup /etc/passwd
sed -i 's|^\(svc-backup:.*:\)/bin/sh$|\1/bin/false|' /etc/passwd
grep svc-backup /etc/passwd

why.q: Why give a service account /bin/false?
o: Nobody can log in as that account interactively
why.x: A service needs an identity, not a login. A non-login shell removes a way in.

title: Find and close world-writable files
story: An audit found files and folders under /srv/apps that anyone can write to. Remove write access for "others" on files and on folders, except the shared folder, which is meant to be open but must be sticky (mode 1777).
goals: No regular file under /srv/apps is writable by others.
No folder is writable by others except /srv/apps/shared.
/srv/apps/shared stays mode 1777.
hints: find /srv/apps -perm -002 lists everything others can write.
Use -type f for files and -type d for folders. chmod o-w removes the write bit for others.
find /srv/apps -type f -perm -002 -exec chmod o-w {} \;  and the same for folders that are not sticky: ! -perm -1000

why.q: Why are world-writable files a risk?
o: Any user on the machine can change them
why.x: If everyone can write, any compromised account can alter the file, and scripts that run it become a way to escalate.

title: Programs that run as root for everyone
story: A scan found programs under /usr/local and /opt with the setuid or setgid bit set. None of them needs it. Remove both bits but keep the programs executable.
goals: No file under /usr/local or /opt has the setuid or setgid bit.
The programs stay executable.
hints: ls -l shows an s instead of x in the owner or group permissions.
find /usr/local /opt -type f -perm -4000 finds setuid files. -perm -2000 finds setgid ones.
find ... -perm -4000 -exec chmod u-s {} \;  and  find ... -perm -2000 -exec chmod g-s {} \;

why.q: What does the setuid bit do?
o: The program runs with its owner's rights, often root
why.x: A setuid root program lets any user run code as root. Few programs should have it, and each one needs a reason.

title: Apply the patch from the ticket
story: A colleague sent a patch file, /root/fix.patch, for /etc/app/app.conf. Apply it. Do not edit the file by hand.
goals: /etc/app/app.conf has MAX_CONN=200 and LOG_LEVEL=warn after the patch.
The other lines of the file are unchanged.
hints: cat /root/fix.patch shows what changes. Lines with - are removed and lines with + are added.
The paths in the patch start with a/ and b/. patch -p1 removes that first folder.
cd /etc/app && patch -p1 < /root/fix.patch
solution:
cat /root/fix.patch
cd /etc/app && patch -p1 < /root/fix.patch
cat /etc/app/app.conf

why.q: Why use patch instead of editing by hand?
o: It applies exactly the described change and can be reviewed
It is the only way to edit files
why.x: A patch file records a precise change, so the same fix can be shared, reviewed and re-applied.

title: The report nobody can read
story: report-gen writes /srv/out/report.txt for the web team, but the file is created with mode 600 so only root can read it. The script sets a strict umask. Fix the script so new reports are readable by others (mode 644) but not writable by them.
goals: After running report-gen, /srv/out/report.txt is mode 644.
hints: ls -l /srv/out/report.txt shows 600. cat /usr/local/bin/report-gen shows a umask line.
umask is a mask of permissions to remove from new files. 077 removes all access for group and others.
sed -i "s/umask 077/umask 022/" /usr/local/bin/report-gen, then run report-gen again.
solution:
ls -l /srv/out/report.txt
sed -i "s/umask 077/umask 022/" /usr/local/bin/report-gen
rm /srv/out/report.txt; report-gen
ls -l /srv/out/report.txt

why.q: What does umask 077 do?
o: New files are private to the owner
why.x: umask removes permission bits from new files. 077 removes everything for group and others.

title: Too many open files
story: The worker needs at least 256 open files, but the launcher sets a low limit. The worker writes its state to /run/worker.status and exits. Fix the limit in the launcher and start the worker so that it keeps running.
goals: worker is running and /run/worker.status says "worker: ok".
The soft limit for open files of the running worker is at least 256.
hints: cat /run/worker.status and cat /usr/local/bin/start-worker. The launcher runs ulimit -n before starting the worker.
ulimit -n shows the limit of your shell. A script sets it only for itself and its children.
sed -i "s/ulimit -n 64/ulimit -n 1024/" /usr/local/bin/start-worker, then run start-worker. Check /proc/PID/limits.
solution:
cat /run/worker.status
sed -i "s/ulimit -n 64/ulimit -n 1024/" /usr/local/bin/start-worker
start-worker
grep "open files" /proc/$(pidof worker)/limits

why.q: Why did raising ulimit in a shell not help the service?
o: The limit applies to that process and what it starts, so it must be set in the launcher
why.x: ulimit sets limits for the current shell and its children. The service must be started with the higher limit.

title: Recover the file that was deleted while open
story: Someone deleted /var/lib/ledger/today.dat while the process ledger-writer still had it open. It holds today's orders. The data is not gone yet: the process can still read it. Save a copy as /root/recovered.dat and leave the process running.
goals: /root/recovered.dat contains the order lines (ORDER-9917 and ORDER-9918).
ledger-writer keeps running.
hints: ls -l /proc/PID/fd lists the files a process has open. Look for "(deleted)".
Get the PID with pidof ledger-writer. Find the fd number whose target says today.dat (deleted).
Open files can be copied through /proc: cp /proc/PID/fd/3 /root/recovered.dat
solution:
ls -l /proc/$(pidof ledger-writer)/fd
cp /proc/$(pidof ledger-writer)/fd/3 /root/recovered.dat
cat /root/recovered.dat

why.q: How could the deleted file still be read?
o: The process kept it open, and /proc/PID/fd gives access
It was restored from the trash
why.x: While a handle is open, the data exists. cp from /proc/PID/fd/N copies it back out.

title: Which database is the running process using?
story: db-proxy was started a week ago with a DB_HOST environment variable. Its config file says something else, and nobody remembers which value is in use. Ask the running process and write the answer as host=NAME into /root/answer.txt.
goals: /root/answer.txt contains host=NAME, with the DB_HOST value the process really has.
hints: A running process keeps its start-up environment in /proc/PID/environ, separated by NUL characters.
tr "\0" "\n" < /proc/PID/environ prints one variable per line.
echo "host=$(tr "\0" "\n" < /proc/$(pidof db-proxy)/environ | sed -n "s/^DB_HOST=//p")" > /root/answer.txt
solution:
tr "\0" "\n" < /proc/$(pidof db-proxy)/environ | grep DB_HOST
echo "host=$(tr "\0" "\n" < /proc/$(pidof db-proxy)/environ | sed -n "s/^DB_HOST=//p")" > /root/answer.txt
cat /root/answer.txt

why.q: Where does a running process keep its environment?
why.x: The environment is fixed when a process starts. /proc/PID/environ shows the real values, which may differ from the config.

title: Change the setting without restarting
story: webd greets visitors with the text in /etc/webd.conf. It reads the file at start and again when it gets the HUP signal. Change the greeting to "hello v2" and make webd use it without restarting the process, because it holds live connections.
goals: /run/webd.state shows "hello v2".
webd keeps the same process id (no restart).
hints: cat /etc/webd.conf and cat /run/webd.state. The process id is in /run/webd.pid.
kill sends any signal. HUP is the traditional "reload your config" signal.
sed -i "s/v1/v2/" /etc/webd.conf; kill -HUP $(cat /run/webd.pid)
solution:
cat /run/webd.state
sed -i "s/v1/v2/" /etc/webd.conf
kill -HUP $(cat /run/webd.pid)
sleep 2; cat /run/webd.state

why.q: What does SIGHUP often mean to a daemon?
why.x: Many daemons treat HUP as reload. It applies new settings without dropping connections.

title: Stop the worker without losing the queue
story: queue-worker keeps messages in memory and writes them to disk only when it receives the normal stop signal (TERM). Stop it so that /var/spool/q/flushed appears. Do not use kill -9.
goals: queue-worker is no longer running.
/var/spool/q/flushed exists, which proves it flushed before exiting.
hints: kill -l lists signals. TERM (15) asks a program to stop; KILL (9) gives it no chance to clean up.
Plain kill PID sends TERM. The worker finishes its current sleep first, so wait a moment.
kill $(pidof queue-worker); sleep 2; ls /var/spool/q
solution:
kill $(pidof queue-worker)
sleep 2
ls /var/spool/q
pidof queue-worker

why.q: Why send SIGTERM before SIGKILL?
o: It lets the program finish its work and clean up
why.x: SIGTERM can be handled, so a worker can save the queue. SIGKILL gives it no chance.

title: The job that froze without crashing
story: etl-job writes the time into /run/etl.hb every second. The file stopped changing, but the process is still listed. Someone paused it with a signal. Resume the same process; do not restart it.
goals: /run/etl.hb is updated again.
etl-job keeps its original process id.
hints: ps -o pid,stat,comm shows the state. T means stopped.
A stopped process is resumed with a signal, not by restarting it.
kill -CONT $(pidof etl-job)
solution:
ps -o pid,stat,comm | grep etl
kill -CONT $(pidof etl-job)
sleep 2; cat /run/etl.hb

why.q: What does kill -CONT do?
o: It resumes a process that was stopped
why.x: A stopped process (SIGSTOP) is frozen but alive. SIGCONT lets it run again.

title: Turn on forwarding and keep it on
story: This machine should route packets between networks, but kernel packet forwarding (net.ipv4.ip_forward) is off. Turn it on now and make it survive a reboot by writing it to /etc/sysctl.conf.
goals: /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward is 1.
/etc/sysctl.conf contains net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1.
hints: cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward shows the live value. sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward shows the same.
sysctl -w sets it now. /etc/sysctl.conf keeps it for the next boot.
echo "net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1" >> /etc/sysctl.conf; sysctl -p
solution:
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
echo "net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1" >> /etc/sysctl.conf
sysctl -p
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward

why.q: Why also write the setting to /etc/sysctl.conf?
why.x: sysctl -w changes the running kernel only. A line in sysctl.conf is applied at every boot.

title: Deleting the file did not free the space
story: /srv/store is nearly full. Someone deleted one data.bin, but the usage did not change. The same 6 MB file has other names (hard links) in other folders. Free the space by removing every name of that file, and keep keep.txt.
goals: /srv/store is under 50 percent full.
keep.txt is still there.
hints: ls -li shows inode numbers and the link count. Files with the same inode are the same data.
Space is freed only when the last name is gone. find /srv/store -name data.bin lists the names.
find /srv/store -name data.bin -exec rm {} \;
solution:
df -h /srv/store
find /srv/store -name data.bin
find /srv/store -name data.bin -exec rm {} \;
df -h /srv/store

why.q: Why did deleting one name free no space?
o: Another hard link still points to the same data
why.x: Data is freed when the last link is gone. Two names for one inode share the same blocks.

title: A 200 MB file that uses almost no disk
story: /srv/vm/disk.img looks like 200 MB in ls -l, but it is a sparse file: most of it is empty space that takes no storage. Report the real disk usage in kilobytes as used_kb=NUMBER in /root/answer.txt.
goals: /root/answer.txt contains used_kb=NUMBER, the blocks the file really uses (as du -k reports).
hints: ls -l shows the apparent size. du shows the blocks used.
du -k FILE prints kilobytes of real usage in the first column.
echo "used_kb=$(du -k /srv/vm/disk.img | cut -f1)" > /root/answer.txt
solution:
ls -l /srv/vm/disk.img
du -k /srv/vm/disk.img
echo "used_kb=$(du -k /srv/vm/disk.img | cut -f1)" > /root/answer.txt
cat /root/answer.txt

why.q: Why is a 200 MB file using almost no disk?
o: Empty holes in a sparse file take no blocks
why.x: A sparse file records its size but only stores the written parts. ls shows the size, du shows the real use.

title: umount says the target is busy
story: /mnt/data must be unmounted, but umount fails with "target is busy". Something is using it. Find it, stop only that program, and unmount. api-server must keep running.
goals: /mnt/data is no longer mounted.
api-server is still running and nightly-report is stopped.
hints: Run umount /mnt/data and read the error. A process whose current directory is inside the mount keeps it busy.
ls -l /proc/*/cwd 2>/dev/null | grep /mnt/data shows who is in there.
kill $(pidof nightly-report); sleep 1; umount /mnt/data
solution:
umount /mnt/data
ls -l /proc/*/cwd 2>/dev/null | grep /mnt/data
kill $(pidof nightly-report)
sleep 1; umount /mnt/data

why.q: Why does umount say the target is busy?
o: A process is using a file or folder on it
why.x: A mount cannot be removed while something uses it, for example a shell inside it. Find the user and stop it.

title: The files vanished when the volume was mounted
story: The old files in /srv/data disappeared after a new volume was mounted on top of it. They are still on disk, hidden underneath. Copy them to /backup/old-data without unmounting the new volume (the app is writing to it).
goals: /backup/old-data/ledger.csv exists with the old content.
The new volume stays mounted on /srv/data.
hints: mount | grep srv shows the volume covering the folder. ls /srv/data shows only the new volume.
A bind mount of / shows the folder without the mounts that cover it: mkdir -p /mnt/rootview; mount --bind / /mnt/rootview
Copy from /mnt/rootview/srv/data, then umount /mnt/rootview.
solution:
mkdir -p /mnt/rootview /backup/old-data
mount --bind / /mnt/rootview
cp -a /mnt/rootview/srv/data/. /backup/old-data/
umount /mnt/rootview

why.q: Why did files disappear after mounting a volume?
o: The mount covers the old folder's contents until unmounted
why.x: Mounting over a folder hides what was there. A bind mount of / shows the files underneath.

title: The script that does not wait for its jobs
story: fetch-all starts three background jobs and then summarises their results, but it summarises too early and says "fetched 0 parts". Fix the script so it prints "fetched 3 parts".
goals: Running fetch-all prints "fetched 3 parts".
Keep the jobs running in parallel (do not run them one after another).
hints: Run fetch-all and read the output. Background jobs started with & run on their own; the script does not wait for them.
The shell builtin wait pauses until all background jobs finish.
sed -i "s/^cat /wait; cat /" /usr/local/bin/fetch-all
solution:
fetch-all
sed -i "s/^cat /wait; cat /" /usr/local/bin/fetch-all
fetch-all

why.q: What does wait do in a script?
o: It waits for background jobs to finish
why.x: Jobs started with & run in the background. Without wait, the script may use their results too early or exit.

title: Two copies run at once despite the lock
story: single-run must never run twice at the same time. It checks for a lock file first, but when two copies start together, both see "no lock" and both run. Make the lock safe. mkdir is atomic: it either creates the directory or fails.
goals: When two copies start at the same moment, only one runs (one line in /run/single.log).
A lone run still works and cleans up its lock.
hints: Read the script: it tests for the lock, sleeps, and only then creates it. Another copy can slip in between.
Replace "test, then create" with one atomic step: if ! mkdir $LOCK 2>/dev/null; then ... exit.
Use sed to change the three lines: the test, the touch and the rm. Use rmdir for a lock that is a directory.
solution:
cat /usr/local/bin/single-run
sed -i 's|^if \[ -e $LOCK \]; then|if ! mkdir $LOCK 2>/dev/null; then|' /usr/local/bin/single-run
sed -i '/^touch $LOCK$/d' /usr/local/bin/single-run
sed -i 's|rm -f $LOCK|rmdir $LOCK|' /usr/local/bin/single-run

why.q: Why is mkdir a better lock than test then touch?
o: It checks and creates in one atomic step
why.x: With test and create, two runs can both pass the test. mkdir either succeeds once or fails, with no gap.

title: Readers see a half-written config
story: update-conf rewrites /etc/app/live.conf by emptying it and then filling it again. For a moment the file is empty, and a program reading it then crashes. Change the script to write a temporary file and rename it into place, so readers see either the old or the new file, never half of one.
goals: While update-conf runs, live.conf is never empty.
When it finishes, live.conf holds a=1, b=2 and c=3.
hints: cat /usr/local/bin/update-conf. The first write truncates the live file.
A rename (mv) on the same filesystem is atomic. Build the new file next to the old one, then mv it over.
sed -i "s|^OUT=.*|OUT=/etc/app/live.conf.new|" the script, then append: echo "mv /etc/app/live.conf.new /etc/app/live.conf" >> the script.
solution:
cat /usr/local/bin/update-conf
sed -i "s|^OUT=.*|OUT=/etc/app/live.conf.new|" /usr/local/bin/update-conf
echo "mv /etc/app/live.conf.new /etc/app/live.conf" >> /usr/local/bin/update-conf

why.q: Why write to a new file and then mv?
o: A rename is atomic, so readers see the old or new file, never half
why.x: A reader that opens the file during a slow write sees a partial file. Renaming a finished file over it is instant.

title: The deploy that says OK after a failed build
story: The deploy script runs a build step. When the build fails, the script carries on, uploads and prints "deploy OK". It must stop at the first failing command.
goals: With /run/build.fail present, deploy exits with an error and does not print "deploy OK".
Without it, deploy still prints "uploading artifact" and "deploy OK".
hints: Create /run/build.fail with touch, run deploy and see it still says OK. Remove the file afterwards.
The shell option set -e stops a script at the first failing command.
Insert it after the first line: sed -i "1a set -e" /usr/local/bin/deploy
solution:
touch /run/build.fail; deploy; rm /run/build.fail
sed -i "1a set -e" /usr/local/bin/deploy
touch /run/build.fail; deploy; rm /run/build.fail

why.q: Why did the deploy print OK after a failed build?
o: The script ignored the failing command's exit code
why.x: Without set -e or an explicit check, a script continues after errors and its last command decides the result.

title: The lock file that is never removed
story: nightly-job creates a lock file and removes it only at the very end. When a step fails, the script exits early and the stale lock blocks every later run. Make sure the lock is removed however the script ends.
goals: After a failed run, /run/nightly.lock does not exist.
After a good run, the lock is gone and "step done" is printed.
hints: cat /usr/local/bin/nightly-job. With set -e the script stops at the failing step and never reaches the rm.
trap runs a command when the script exits, for any reason: trap "COMMAND" EXIT
sed -i '2a trap "rm -f /run/nightly.lock" EXIT' /usr/local/bin/nightly-job
solution:
cat /usr/local/bin/nightly-job
sed -i '2a trap "rm -f /run/nightly.lock" EXIT' /usr/local/bin/nightly-job
rm -f /run/nightly.lock

why.q: What does trap ... EXIT do?
o: It runs a command when the script ends, even after an error
why.x: A trap on EXIT removes the lock file however the script ends, so a crash does not leave it behind.

title: Copy a tree and keep owners, dates and links
story: Copy the release folder /srv/src to /srv/dst for the new host. The copy must keep each file's owner, its modification time and the symlink "latest". A plain cp -r loses these.
goals: /srv/dst has the same files as /srv/src.
Owners and modification times are the same, and "latest" is still a symlink.
hints: ls -l --time-style may not exist here; use stat -c "%u %Y %N" FILE to see owner, mtime and link target.
cp has an archive option that keeps everything: -a.
mkdir -p /srv/dst; cp -a /srv/src/. /srv/dst/   (or: tar -C /srv/src -cf - . | tar -C /srv/dst -xf -)
solution:
mkdir -p /srv/dst
cp -a /srv/src/. /srv/dst/
stat -c "%u %Y %N" /srv/dst/conf/app.conf /srv/dst/latest

why.q: What does cp -a keep that a plain cp does not?
why.x: -a is archive mode: it copies recursively and preserves attributes, which a faithful copy needs.

title: Who spent the most?
story: orders.csv lists order id, customer id and amount. customers.csv maps customer id to a name. Find the customer with the highest total spend and write top=NAME into /root/answer.txt.
goals: /root/answer.txt contains top=NAME for the customer with the largest total.
hints: head /srv/sales/orders.csv /srv/sales/customers.csv shows the columns. There are no header lines.
awk can add up amounts per customer id in an array: s[$2]+=$3
Read customers.csv first (NR==FNR), then orders.csv, and look up the name at the end.
solution:
awk -F, 'NR==FNR{n[$1]=$2; next} {s[$2]+=$3} END{for(c in s) if(s[c]>m){m=s[c]; b=c}; print "top=" n[b]}' /srv/sales/customers.csv /srv/sales/orders.csv > /root/answer.txt
cat /root/answer.txt

why.q: Why join two files with awk?
o: awk can only read one file
To turn an id into a name using a lookup table
why.x: Read the small file into an array first, then use it to translate ids while reading the big file.

title: How many different email domains signed up?
story: signups.txt has one signup per line, in the form: date, text, email=ADDRESS, plan=PLAN. Other addresses appear in the text. Count how many different domains appear in the email= fields and write domains=NUMBER into /root/answer.txt.
goals: /root/answer.txt contains domains=NUMBER, counting only the email= fields.
hints: head /srv/data/signups.txt shows the format. grep -o prints only the matching part of each line.
grep -o "email=[^ ]*" gets the field. sed "s/.*@//" keeps what follows the @.
grep -o "email=[^ ]*" FILE | sed "s/.*@//" | sort -u | wc -l
solution:
grep -o "email=[^ ]*" /srv/data/signups.txt | sed "s/.*@//" | sort -u | wc -l
echo "domains=$(grep -o "email=[^ ]*" /srv/data/signups.txt | sed "s/.*@//" | sort -u | wc -l)" > /root/answer.txt

why.q: Why strip the part before @?
o: Domains are the text after @, and duplicates then collapse
why.x: sed removes the user part, and sort -u counts each domain once.

title: Read a JSON field without jq
story: There is no jq on this machine. /srv/api/response.json is one line of JSON. Pull out the value of the "version" key (not "api_version") and write version=VALUE into /root/answer.txt.
goals: /root/answer.txt contains version=2.4.1.
hints: cat /srv/api/response.json. Two keys end in "version"; you want the exact key "version".
sed -n can print only a captured part: s/.*"key":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p
The quote before version excludes api_version, because there the character before "version" is an underscore.
solution:
cat /srv/api/response.json
echo "version=$(sed -n 's/.*"version":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' /srv/api/response.json)" > /root/answer.txt
cat /root/answer.txt

why.q: Why is sed fragile on JSON?
o: JSON can change spacing and nesting, which breaks the pattern
why.x: A pattern that fits one layout can fail on another. A real parser is safer when available.

title: Decode the secret and keep it private
story: The database password is stored base64-encoded in /etc/app/secret.b64. Decode it into /root/db-password.txt exactly (no extra characters), and make the file readable only by its owner.
goals: /root/db-password.txt holds the decoded password.
The file mode is 600.
hints: base64 -d decodes. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption.
Redirect the output into the file. Then restrict the file with chmod.
base64 -d /etc/app/secret.b64 > /root/db-password.txt; chmod 600 /root/db-password.txt
solution:
cat /etc/app/secret.b64
base64 -d /etc/app/secret.b64 > /root/db-password.txt
chmod 600 /root/db-password.txt

why.q: Why chmod 600 the decoded file?
o: Only the owner should read a password
why.x: Anything that decodes to a secret needs private permissions at once, before anyone else can read it.

title: Which download is corrupted?
story: Three release files were downloaded to /srv/downloads, with a SHA256SUMS list from the publisher. One file does not match its checksum. Write its name as bad=FILENAME into /root/answer.txt. Do not delete anything.
goals: /root/answer.txt contains bad=NAME for the file that fails verification.
hints: cat /srv/downloads/SHA256SUMS shows the expected checksums.
sha256sum -c FILE checks every file listed and prints OK or FAILED. Run it from the downloads folder.
cd /srv/downloads; sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS 2>/dev/null | grep -v ": OK" | cut -d: -f1
solution:
cd /srv/downloads
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
echo "bad=$(sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS 2>/dev/null | grep -v ': OK$' | cut -d: -f1)" > /root/answer.txt
cat /root/answer.txt

why.q: What does sha256sum -c prove?
o: That the file is safe to run
That each file matches the recorded hash
why.x: A matching hash shows the file is unchanged. A mismatch means damage or tampering.

title: Build a block list from the auth log
story: The auth log shows many failed SSH logins. Write the addresses with 5 or more "Failed password" lines, one per line and sorted, into /root/blocklist.txt. Successful logins must not count.
goals: /root/blocklist.txt lists every address with at least 5 failed logins, sorted, one per line.
No address with fewer failures is listed.
hints: head /var/log/auth.log. Only lines with "Failed password" count.
grep -oE "[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+" pulls out addresses. sort | uniq -c counts them.
awk "$1>=5 {print $2}" keeps the frequent ones.
solution:
grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | grep -oE "[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+" | sort | uniq -c | awk '$1>=5{print $2}' | sort > /root/blocklist.txt
cat /root/blocklist.txt

why.q: Why count failures per address?
o: A few failures are normal, many from one address are an attack
why.x: Counting and a threshold (five or more) picks out brute-force sources without blocking honest typos.

title: Build a tiny chroot jail
story: Create a minimal root file system at /jail so that chroot /jail /bin/cat /etc/motd prints "inside the jail". It needs a copy of busybox, a cat link to it and the motd file. It must not contain a copy of the host's /etc/passwd.
goals: chroot /jail /bin/cat /etc/motd prints: inside the jail
/jail/etc/passwd does not exist.
hints: A chroot only sees what is inside it, so the program and everything it needs must be copied in. busybox is one static file.
Make /jail/bin and /jail/etc, copy /bin/busybox into /jail/bin, and link cat to it: ln -s busybox /jail/bin/cat
Write the motd file: echo "inside the jail" > /jail/etc/motd
solution:
mkdir -p /jail/bin /jail/etc
cp /bin/busybox /jail/bin/
ln -s busybox /jail/bin/cat
echo "inside the jail" > /jail/etc/motd
chroot /jail /bin/cat /etc/motd

why.q: What does chroot do?
o: It changes the root of a process to a folder
why.x: After chroot, the process sees the chosen folder as /. It can only use tools you copied inside.

title: The cache volume is too small
story: /var/cache/app is a small in-memory volume that the app has nearly filled. It needs at least 8 MB. Resize it without unmounting, so the cached file survives.
goals: /var/cache/app is at least 8 MB in size.
cache.bin is still there.
hints: df -k /var/cache/app shows the size and use. mount | grep cache shows the options (size=2m).
A tmpfs can be resized live with a remount.
mount -o remount,size=8m /var/cache/app
solution:
df -k /var/cache/app
mount -o remount,size=8m /var/cache/app
df -k /var/cache/app

why.q: Where does a tmpfs live?
o: In memory, with a size limit you can change
why.x: A tmpfs is RAM-backed. mount -o remount,size=8m changes the limit without losing files.

title: Which request killed the app?
story: crash.log has start and finish lines for requests and, somewhere, a segfault line from the kernel. Find the request that started just before the crash and write req=REQ-NUMBER into /root/answer.txt.
goals: /root/answer.txt contains req=ID of the request on the line just before the segfault.
hints: grep -n segfault /var/log/app/crash.log shows the line number of the crash.
grep -B1 prints the matching line and the line before it.
grep -B1 segfault FILE | head -1 | grep -o "REQ-[0-9]*"
solution:
grep -B1 segfault /var/log/app/crash.log
echo "req=$(grep -B1 segfault /var/log/app/crash.log | head -1 | grep -o 'REQ-[0-9]*')" > /root/answer.txt
cat /root/answer.txt

why.q: Why use grep -B1?
o: It also prints the line before each match
why.x: -B N prints N lines before the match, so you see the request that came just before the crash.

title: The slowest request
story: latency.txt has one latency in milliseconds per line. Find the largest value and write max_ms=NUMBER into /root/answer.txt. A plain sort puts 95 after 2048, because it sorts as text.
goals: /root/answer.txt contains max_ms=NUMBER with the real maximum.
hints: sort FILE | tail -1 gives the wrong answer here. Sorting as text compares character by character.
sort -n sorts by number.
echo "max_ms=$(sort -n /srv/data/latency.txt | tail -1)" > /root/answer.txt
solution:
sort /srv/data/latency.txt | tail -1
sort -n /srv/data/latency.txt | tail -1
echo "max_ms=$(sort -n /srv/data/latency.txt | tail -1)" > /root/answer.txt

why.q: Why did plain sort give the wrong slowest request?
o: It sorts as text, so 9 comes after 100
why.x: Text sorting compares character by character. sort -n compares numbers.

title: Stop the job and everything it started
story: batch-parent starts two batch-child workers and waits for them. Stop the whole job. If you kill only the parent, the children keep running. api-server must keep running.
goals: No batch-parent and no batch-child process is running.
api-server is still running.
hints: ps shows the family. Killing the parent does not kill its children.
pidof accepts several names: pidof batch-parent batch-child
kill $(pidof batch-parent batch-child)
solution:
ps | grep batch
kill $(pidof batch-parent batch-child)
ps | grep batch

why.q: Why did the children keep running after the parent stopped?
o: Killing a parent does not stop the processes it started
why.x: Child processes continue and get a new parent. Stop the whole group, or children too.

title: Which process keeps writing to this log?
story: /var/log/mystery.log grows every second and nobody knows who writes it. Three writer programs run, and none shows the file name in its command line. Find the owner and write owner=NAME (the process name) into /root/answer.txt.
goals: /root/answer.txt contains owner=NAME for the process that has mystery.log open.
hints: Every open file of a process appears as a link in /proc/PID/fd.
Loop over the processes: for p in /proc/[0-9]*; do ls -l $p/fd 2>/dev/null | grep -q mystery.log && echo $p; done
The process name is in /proc/PID/comm.
solution:
for p in /proc/[0-9]*; do ls -l $p/fd 2>/dev/null | grep -q mystery.log && echo "owner=$(cat $p/comm)" > /root/answer.txt; done
cat /root/answer.txt

why.q: How can you find which process has a file open?
o: Look through /proc/PID/fd for links to that file
why.x: Each process lists its open files in /proc/PID/fd. The one that links to the log is the writer.

title: The unit that points at the wrong binary
story: The ledger service will not start. Its unit file was written by hand and the program lives somewhere else. Fix the unit and start ledger with systemctl. This lab uses a small imitation of systemctl, not the real systemd.
goals: ledger is active.
The unit file points at the real program.
hints: systemctl status ledger shows the failure. journalctl -u ledger shows why.
Find the program: ls /opt/ledger/bin
Edit ExecStart in /etc/systemd/system/ledger.service, run systemctl daemon-reload, then systemctl start ledger.
solution:
systemctl status ledger
journalctl -u ledger
sed -i "s#/opt/ledger/ledgerd#/opt/ledger/bin/ledgerd#" /etc/systemd/system/ledger.service
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl start ledger
systemctl status ledger

why.q: Why did the unit fail?
o: ExecStart named a file that does not exist
why.x: The service manager starts exactly the path in ExecStart. A wrong path ends with status 203/EXEC.

title: Works now, gone after the reboot
story: billing runs right now because someone started it by hand. After the last reboot it was down for an hour. Make sure billing starts by itself at boot, without stopping it now. This lab uses a small imitation of systemctl.
