goals: billing is running now.
billing is enabled, so a reboot starts it again.
hints: systemctl is-enabled billing tells you whether it starts at boot.
systemctl enable billing creates the link that boot follows.
Do not stop it: it must keep running.
solution:
systemctl is-enabled billing
systemctl enable billing
systemctl is-enabled billing

why.q: What is the difference between start and enable?
o: start runs it now, enable makes it start at boot
why.x: start affects the running system. enable adds the link that boot follows. You usually want both.

title: I edited the unit, but nothing changed
story: api must listen on port 9090 now. Someone changed the unit file and restarted the service, but api still reports port 8080. The change never took effect. Make api run with port 9090.
goals: /run/api.args says --port 9090.
api is active.
hints: cat /run/api.args shows the arguments the running api really got.
systemctl status api prints a warning about the unit file.
systemd keeps its own loaded copy of a unit. Reload it with systemctl daemon-reload, then restart the service.
solution:
cat /run/api.args
systemctl status api
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart api
cat /run/api.args

why.q: Why did the edit not take effect after a restart?
o: systemd uses its loaded copy until daemon-reload
why.x: systemd keeps the unit definitions in memory. After editing a unit file, systemctl daemon-reload loads the new version.

title: The environment file that is not there
story: payments will not start. Its unit loads settings from an environment file, and the service refuses to run without PAY_MODE. The file exists, but not where the unit looks for it.
goals: payments is active.
/run/payments.mode says live.
hints: journalctl -u payments says it failed to load the environment file.
Find the real file: find /etc/payments -type f
Fix the EnvironmentFile line, run systemctl daemon-reload and start payments.
solution:
journalctl -u payments
find /etc/payments -type f
sed -i "s#/etc/payments/payments.env#/etc/payments/env.d/payments.env#" /etc/systemd/system/payments.service
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl start payments
cat /run/payments.mode

why.q: What does EnvironmentFile= do?
o: It loads variables from a file for the service
why.x: systemd reads KEY=value lines from the file and gives them to the process. A wrong path stops the start.

title: A crash that nobody noticed
story: datasync crashed at 03:10 with a lost database connection and stayed down until morning. It crashes the first two times it starts and then runs fine, so a restart policy would have saved the night. Add one and bring the service up.
goals: datasync survives its early crashes and keeps running.
The unit has Restart=on-failure.
hints: journalctl -u datasync shows the crash. systemctl status datasync shows it is failed.
Add a Restart=on-failure line in the [Service] section of /etc/systemd/system/datasync.service.
Run systemctl daemon-reload, then systemctl start datasync. Wait a few seconds and check the status again.
solution:
journalctl -u datasync
sed -i "/^ExecStart/a Restart=on-failure" /etc/systemd/system/datasync.service
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl start datasync
sleep 5
systemctl status datasync

why.q: What does Restart=on-failure do?
o: It restarts the service if it exits with an error
why.x: With a restart policy a crash is handled automatically, with a pause between tries.

title: The service account that does not exist
story: metrics-agent must run as the user metrics, with uid 1001. Its unit names the user metrics-agent and the service fails with a USER error. Fix the unit so the agent runs as the right account.
goals: metrics-agent is active.
It runs with uid 1001.
hints: journalctl -u metrics-agent says no such process at step USER.
grep metrics /etc/passwd lists the real account name.
Fix User= in the unit, run systemctl daemon-reload and start the service.
solution:
journalctl -u metrics-agent
grep metrics /etc/passwd
sed -i "s/^User=.*/User=metrics/" /etc/systemd/system/metrics-agent.service
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl start metrics-agent

why.q: What does User= in a unit do?
o: It names the owner of the file
It runs the service as that account
why.x: systemd drops to that user before starting the program. If the user does not exist, the start fails at the USER step.

title: The service somebody masked
story: queue-worker refuses to start: "Unit is masked". A teammate masked it during an incident last month and never undid it. It must run, and it must start at boot.
goals: queue-worker is active.
queue-worker is enabled.
hints: systemctl status queue-worker says it is masked. A masked unit is a link to /dev/null.
systemctl unmask queue-worker removes the block.
Then enable and start it. systemctl enable --now does both.
solution:
systemctl status queue-worker
systemctl unmask queue-worker
systemctl enable --now queue-worker
systemctl status queue-worker

why.q: What does masking a unit do?
o: It makes it impossible to start, even by hand
why.x: A masked unit links to /dev/null. Unmask removes the block.

title: The drop-in that quietly wins
story: db-sync must run in live mode. The main unit file says live, yet the job reports dry-run and changes nothing. Somebody left an override file from an old ticket. Make db-sync run live without editing the main unit.
goals: /run/dbsync.mode says live.
db-sync is active.
hints: systemctl cat db-sync prints the unit and every drop-in that applies to it.
The file under /etc/systemd/system/db-sync.service.d/ sets the mode.
Remove or fix the override, run systemctl daemon-reload and restart db-sync.
solution:
systemctl cat db-sync
rm /etc/systemd/system/db-sync.service.d/ticket-4417.conf
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart db-sync
cat /run/dbsync.mode

why.q: How do drop-in files work?
o: Their settings are added to the main unit and can override it
why.x: Files in unit.service.d/*.conf are merged in. systemctl cat shows the full result.

title: Start request repeated too quickly
story: indexer keeps crashing right after it starts, and systemd gave up: the unit shows failed with a start limit. The crash comes from a typo in its configuration. Fix the cause, clear the failed state and start it.
goals: indexer is active and stays up.
/etc/indexer.conf has a valid value for workers.
hints: journalctl -u indexer shows the crash message and the start limit.
The program prints what is wrong with the config. The value for workers must be a number.
Fix /etc/indexer.conf, then systemctl reset-failed indexer and systemctl start indexer.
solution:
journalctl -u indexer -n 20
sed -i "s/workers=.*/workers=4/" /etc/indexer.conf
systemctl reset-failed indexer
systemctl start indexer
systemctl status indexer

why.q: Why did systemd stop restarting the service?
o: It started too often in a short time
why.x: After several fast restarts systemd gives up. Fix the cause, then use systemctl reset-failed.

title: The app that needs its database first
story: orders refuses to start because its pre-start check cannot find the database. The database unit exists but is stopped and is not enabled. Both must run now, and both must come back after a reboot.
goals: orders and orders-db are active.
Both units are enabled.
hints: journalctl -u orders shows the failed pre-start check.
Start the database first: systemctl start orders-db.
Enable both units, then start orders. A simulated reboot must bring both back.
solution:
journalctl -u orders
systemctl enable --now orders-db
systemctl enable --now orders
systemctl status orders

why.q: What does ExecStartPre= do?
o: It runs a command before the main program and must succeed
why.x: If the pre-start command fails, the service does not start. Here it needs the database.

title: The app host has no route to the database
story: The orders app on this host cannot reach the database at 10.0.2.10 port 5432. The database sits behind a router at 10.0.1.254. Other teams reach it fine. The lab builds a small private network inside the machine with network namespaces (inns NAME command runs a command inside one; ls /run/ns lists them).
goals: wget http://10.0.2.10:5432/ answers "orders-db ready".
The fix is a route, not a change on the router or the database.
hints: ip route lists this host's routes. Is there one for 10.0.2.0/24?
ping 10.0.1.254 works (the router is on the local network), ping 10.0.2.10 does not.
Add the route: ip route add 10.0.2.0/24 via 10.0.1.254

why.q: How does a host know where to send a packet for another network?
o: It checks its routing table for a matching route
why.x: Without a route for 10.0.2.0/24 and without a default route the host has nowhere to send it.

title: The router that does not forward
story: The route to the database is in place, yet connections to 10.0.2.10 just time out. Pings to the router answer. A teammate rebuilt the router last night. Find out why traffic stops there and fix it on the router. The lab builds a small private network inside the machine with network namespaces (inns NAME command runs a command inside one; ls /run/ns lists them).
goals: wget http://10.0.2.10:5432/ answers "orders-db ready".
The host routes are left as they are.
hints: ping 10.0.1.254 answers, ping 10.0.2.10 does not. The packets reach the router and stop.
On a Linux router, /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward must be 1. Look inside the router: inns router cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
Turn it on: inns router sh -c "echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward"
solution:
ping -c1 10.0.1.254
ping -c1 -W1 10.0.2.10
inns router cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
inns router sh -c "echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward"
wget -qO- http://10.0.2.10:5432/

why.q: What must be on for a Linux machine to act as a router?
why.x: By default Linux drops packets not meant for itself. ip_forward=1 turns on forwarding.

title: Requests arrive, answers never come back
story: Connections from this host to the database at 10.0.2.10 time out. The route and the router are fine. The database team says their server logs show every request arriving. The replies must be getting lost on the way back. The lab builds a small private network inside the machine with network namespaces (inns NAME command runs a command inside one; ls /run/ns lists them).
goals: wget http://10.0.2.10:5432/ answers "orders-db ready".
Fix the problem where it is, on the database side.
hints: A request needs a path in both directions. Look at the database machine's own routes: inns db ip route
The database has an address in 10.0.2.0/24 only. It has no way to reach 10.0.1.1 (this host).
Give it a default route through the router: inns db ip route add default via 10.0.2.254
solution:
ip route
inns db ip route
inns db ip route add default via 10.0.2.254
wget -qO- http://10.0.2.10:5432/

why.q: Why can a server receive requests but not answer?
o: Its replies have no route back
why.x: A TCP connection needs both directions. If the server cannot route to the client's network, the answer is lost.

title: The mask that is too small
story: The storefront at 10.0.3.20 is on the same network as this host, yet nothing can reach it: "Network is unreachable". The network is 10.0.3.0/24. Check how this host's interface h-w was configured. The lab builds a small private network inside the machine with network namespaces (inns NAME command runs a command inside one; ls /run/ns lists them).
goals: wget http://10.0.3.20:8080/ answers "storefront ok".
h-w keeps the address 10.0.3.1 with the right mask.
hints: ip addr show h-w shows the address and its mask. What does /30 cover?
A /30 holds only four addresses, so 10.0.3.20 is "not on the local network" for this host.
Remove the address and add it again with /24: ip addr del 10.0.3.1/30 dev h-w; ip addr add 10.0.3.1/24 dev h-w
solution:
ip addr show h-w
ip addr del 10.0.3.1/30 dev h-w
ip addr add 10.0.3.1/24 dev h-w
wget -qO- http://10.0.3.20:8080/

why.q: What does /30 mean?
o: Only four addresses form the local network
why.x: The prefix length says how many bits are the network. /30 leaves 2 bits for hosts, so 10.0.3.20 is not local.

title: The network interface somebody turned off
story: The storefront at 10.0.3.20 is not answering from this host. The link h-w to the storefront network was switched off during maintenance and nobody turned it back on. The lab builds a small private network inside the machine with network namespaces (inns NAME command runs a command inside one; ls /run/ns lists them).
goals: wget http://10.0.3.20:8080/ answers "storefront ok".
hints: ip link show h-w prints the state of the interface. Look for DOWN.
ip addr show h-w also shows the address, which stays configured.
Bring it up: ip link set h-w up
solution:
ip link show h-w
ip link set h-w up
wget -qO- http://10.0.3.20:8080/

why.q: What does ip link set up do?
o: It brings the interface into service
why.x: A link can be administratively down. Until it is up, no traffic passes and its routes disappear.

title: Listening, but only on the loopback address
story: The storefront process runs and answers on its own machine, but nobody else can reach it at 10.0.3.20:8080. start-web starts it. Make it reachable from this host. The lab builds a small private network inside the machine with network namespaces (inns NAME command runs a command inside one; ls /run/ns lists them).
goals: wget http://10.0.3.20:8080/ answers "storefront ok".
The storefront keeps listening on port 8080.
hints: Inside the machine: inns web netstat -ln shows the address the server listens on. 127.0.0.1 means loopback only.
cat /usr/local/bin/start-web shows the bind address.
Change the address to 0.0.0.0, stop the old httpd (kill $(pidof httpd)) and run start-web again.
solution:
inns web netstat -ln
sed -i "s/BIND=127.0.0.1/BIND=0.0.0.0/" /usr/local/bin/start-web
kill $(pidof httpd)
start-web
wget -qO- http://10.0.3.20:8080/

why.q: Which address makes a service reachable from other machines?
why.x: 127.0.0.1 only accepts local clients. 0.0.0.0 means all addresses.

title: The route that points at the wrong gateway
story: The orders app cannot reach the database at 10.0.2.10. Somebody added a static route for 10.0.2.0/24 by hand, but the gateway address in it is a typo. The router is at 10.0.1.254. The lab builds a small private network inside the machine with network namespaces (inns NAME command runs a command inside one; ls /run/ns lists them).
goals: wget http://10.0.2.10:5432/ answers "orders-db ready".
There is exactly one route for 10.0.2.0/24, via the router.
hints: ip route shows the route and its gateway. Then ping the gateway: it does not answer.
ip neigh show (or arp) lists hosts this machine has talked to. 10.0.1.253 stays unresolved.
Replace the route: ip route replace 10.0.2.0/24 via 10.0.1.254
solution:
ip route
ping -c1 -W1 10.0.1.253
ip route replace 10.0.2.0/24 via 10.0.1.254
wget -qO- http://10.0.2.10:5432/

why.q: Why does a route to a wrong gateway time out?
o: No machine answers for that address, so packets are never delivered
why.x: The next hop must exist on the local network. A typo gives a gateway no one owns.

title: The server that is not plugged into the bridge
story: web (10.0.9.2) and db (10.0.9.3) should talk to each other through the bridge br0 on this machine. web can reach the bridge, db cannot be reached from web. The cables (veth ports p-web and p-db) both exist and are up. The lab builds a small private network inside the machine with network namespaces (inns NAME command runs a command inside one; ls /run/ns lists them).
goals: web can ping db at 10.0.9.3.
Both p-web and p-db are ports of br0.
hints: ls /sys/class/net/br0/brif lists the ports attached to the bridge br0. Which one is missing?
A port that is not attached to the bridge is just a loose cable.
Attach it: brctl addif br0 p-db
solution:
ls /sys/class/net/br0/brif
inns web ping -c1 -W2 10.0.9.3
brctl addif br0 p-db
inns web ping -c1 10.0.9.3

why.q: What does a bridge do?
o: It joins its ports into one layer 2 network
why.x: Frames move between ports of the same bridge. A port not attached is not part of that network.

title: Which program owns port 9101?
story: A security scan found something listening on port 9101 and nobody knows whose it is. Three small programs run on this machine, and none is called anything obvious. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.
hints: netstat -tln shows the listening ports, but not who owns them.
ps -o pid,ppid,args lists each process with its parent. The listener nc has a parent: the script that started it.
Find the nc line with -p 9101, then read the name of its parent script.
solution:
netstat -tln
ps -o pid,ppid,args
# the nc with -p 9101 has a parent script
Answer: metrics-exporter
ask: Which program (give its file name) listens on port 9101?

why.q: Why look at the parent of the listening process?
o: The script that started nc is the program you want to name
why.x: A tiny helper (nc) listens, but the script that spawns it is the service whose owner you must ask.

title: Who owns the biggest export?
story: The export folder /srv/exports ate most of the disk last night. Before anyone deletes anything, the team wants to know who created the largest file, so they can ask. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.
hints: find /srv/exports -type f lists every file. Add -exec ls -l {} + to see sizes and owners.
ls -lS sorts by size, largest first. The owner is the third column.
The largest file is in one of the sub-folders, not at the top.
solution:
find /srv/exports -type f -exec ls -l {} +
Answer: bruno
ask: Which user owns the largest file under /srv/exports?

why.q: What does ls -l show in its third column?
why.x: The columns are mode, links, owner, group, size, date and name. The owner is the third one.

title: What did the shop run out of?
story: The shop service crashed at midnight. Its log is long and mostly routine. Somewhere in it, one line says why it stopped. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.
hints: The log is /var/log/shop.log. grep -n FATAL /var/log/shop.log finds the serious lines.
tail -n 20 shows the last lines before the crash.
The FATAL line names a resource and a file it could not write.
solution:
grep -n FATAL /var/log/shop.log
tail -n 20 /var/log/shop.log
Answer: disk space
ask: What did the shop service run out of when it crashed? (one or two words)

why.q: Why start with grep FATAL in a long log?
o: Serious lines are few and name the cause
why.x: Logs are mostly routine. Searching for FATAL or ERROR jumps to the lines that matter.

title: Which scheduled job fails?
story: A teammate says "the nightly jobs are flaky". Every job logs one line per run to /var/log/cron-jobs.log with its exit code. Four jobs run every night. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.
hints: cat /var/log/cron-jobs.log shows the lines. Each ends with rc=N.
rc=0 means success. grep -v "rc=0" shows only the failures.
Count: grep -c on the job name shows how often it failed.
solution:
grep -v "rc=0" /var/log/cron-jobs.log
Answer: nightly-export
ask: Which job fails (exit code not 0)? Give its name.

why.q: What does exit code 0 mean?
why.x: By convention 0 means success and anything else is an error, so filtering rc=0 out shows the failures.

title: Where does the traffic die?
story: Connections from this host to the database at 10.0.2.10 time out. The route exists. Pings to the router at 10.0.1.254 work, pings to the database do not. Inside the machine there are private networks: inns NAME command runs a command inside one (ls /run/ns lists them). Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.
hints: ping -c1 10.0.1.254 works and ping -c1 -W1 10.0.2.10 does not, so the packets die at or after the router.
Look inside the router: inns router ip route and inns router ip addr show where it is connected.
A Linux machine forwards packets only when /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward is 1.
solution:
ping -c1 10.0.1.254
ping -c1 -W1 10.0.2.10
inns router cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
Answer: net.ipv4.ip_forward is 0 on the router
ask: Which setting on the router stops the traffic? Name the setting or the file.

why.q: How do you find where packets die?
o: Check the colour of the cable
Test each hop in turn and compare what works
why.x: If the router answers but the next machine does not, the problem sits at or after the router.

title: Which endpoint is slow on average?
story: Users say the site "feels slow". The access log /var/log/access.log has one line per request: method, path, status and the time in milliseconds. One path is much slower than the rest on average, even though it is not the busiest. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.
hints: Each line looks like: GET /path 200 123 (the last number is milliseconds).
awk can sum and count per path: awk '{s[$2]+=$4; n[$2]++} END {for (p in s) print s[p]/n[p], p}' /var/log/access.log
Sort the result: add | sort -n and read the last line.
solution:
awk '{s[$2]+=$4; n[$2]++} END {for (p in s) print s[p]/n[p], p}' /var/log/access.log | sort -n
Answer: /api/search
ask: Which path has the highest average response time?

why.q: Why compare averages instead of one slow request?
o: One slow request can be luck, an average shows a pattern
why.x: An average per path points to a path that is consistently slow.

title: Who deleted the data folder?
story: /srv/data is gone. The auth log /var/log/auth.log records every sudo command with the user who ran it. Several people used sudo yesterday. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.
hints: grep sudo /var/log/auth.log shows the sudo lines.
Search for the command: grep "rm -rf" /var/log/auth.log
The user name comes before the colon after "sudo:".
solution:
grep "rm -rf" /var/log/auth.log
Answer: deploy
ask: Which user ran the command that removed /srv/data?

why.q: Where do sudo commands get recorded?
o: In the auth log with the user's name
why.x: sudo logs who ran which command as root, which is the first place to look in an audit.

title: Which process holds the memory?
story: free shows memory running low on this machine. Three background programs run. One of them holds far more memory than the others, while using almost no CPU, so top by CPU hides it. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.
hints: free shows the totals. top -b -n1 lists processes; the VSZ and RSS columns are about memory.
Every process has /proc/PID/status with a VmRSS line.
Compare the three scripts in /usr/local/bin by their memory, not their CPU.
solution:
free
top -b -n1 | head -15
Answer: report-builder
ask: Which program has the largest memory footprint? Give its name.

why.q: Which column shows the memory a process really uses?
why.x: RSS counts memory held in RAM. VSZ counts address space, which can be much larger.

title: Which process leaks file descriptors?
story: Opening files fails with "Too many open files" every few days. Four background programs run. One of them opens files and never closes them. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.
hints: Each process lists its open files in /proc/PID/fd. ls /proc/PID/fd | wc -l counts them.
Loop over all processes: for p in /proc/[0-9]*; do echo "$(ls $p/fd 2>/dev/null | wc -l) $p"; done | sort -n
Then read the name: cat /proc/PID/cmdline | tr "\0" " "
solution:
for p in /proc/[0-9]*; do echo "$(ls $p/fd 2>/dev/null | wc -l) $p"; done | sort -n | tail -3
Answer: uploader
ask: Which program holds the most open file descriptors? Give its name.

why.q: Where can you count a process's open files?
why.x: Each open file or socket is a link in /proc/PID/fd. A very long list marks a leak.

title: Which directory has all the tiny files?
story: The spool volume reports "No space left on device" while df shows free blocks: it ran out of inodes. Under /var/spool there are several queue directories, and one of them holds almost all the files. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.
hints: df -i shows inode use. Each file costs one inode.
Count files per directory: for d in /var/spool/*; do echo "$(ls $d | wc -l) $d"; done
Sort the numbers and read the largest.
solution:
df -i /var/spool
for d in /var/spool/*; do echo "$(ls $d | wc -l) $d"; done | sort -n
Answer: mailq
ask: Which directory under /var/spool holds the most files? Give its name.

why.q: Why can a disk be full while df shows free space?
o: The file system ran out of inodes
why.x: Every file needs an inode. Millions of tiny files use them all.

title: Where did the access key leak?
story: A scanner flagged an access key (it starts with AKIA) in the code tree /srv/app. Security needs to know which file holds it before they rotate the key. There are many files and old backups. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.
hints: grep -r "AKIA" /srv/app searches the whole tree. -l prints only file names.
Backups and old copies matter: do not skip hidden or .bak files.
Read the name from the grep output.
solution:
grep -rl AKIA /srv/app
Answer: settings.bak (in /srv/app/old)
ask: Which file contains the key? Give the file name.

why.q: Why search backups and old copies for secrets?
o: A leaked key often lives in a forgotten file
why.x: grep -r finds secrets wherever they are. A key in a .bak file is still a leaked key.

title: Silent drops: which network is blackholed?
story: Connections to some addresses fail instantly, and connections to one network just hang forever with no error. A hang with no error usually means packets are dropped silently. Look at this machine's routing table. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.
hints: ip route lists every route. Some routes have a special type word instead of "via".
blackhole drops packets silently. unreachable and prohibit answer with an error right away.
Read the network that has the word blackhole.
solution:
ip route
Answer: 10.6.0.0/24
ask: Which network has the blackhole route? Give it like 10.1.0.0/24.

why.q: What is different about a blackhole route?
o: It drops packets silently, so connections hang
why.x: unreachable and prohibit answer with an ICMP error. A blackhole gives no signal, so clients time out.

title: The release script that fails three ways
story: The release script /opt/app/deploy.sh was written on a laptop and copied over. It will not run on this server, and each time one problem is fixed another shows up. Several things are wrong at once. Fixing the first one will not be enough.
goals: Running /opt/app/deploy.sh writes "deployed v42" to /run/deploy.out.
The script runs directly, as ./deploy.sh would.
hints: Run it and read the error: ls -l /opt/app/deploy.sh shows the permissions, head -1 shows the first line.
Three separate problems: permissions, line endings (cat -A shows ^M), and the interpreter named in the first line (which shells exist? ls /bin/sh /bin/bash).
Fix each: chmod +x, sed -i "s/\r$//" file, and make the first line #!/bin/sh.
solution:
chmod +x /opt/app/deploy.sh
sed -i "s/\r$//" /opt/app/deploy.sh
sed -i "1s|.*|#!/bin/sh|" /opt/app/deploy.sh
/opt/app/deploy.sh
cat /run/deploy.out

why.q: Why was it important to fix the three faults in order of the error messages?
o: Each fix reveals the next problem hidden behind it
why.x: A script fails at the first problem. After you fix it, the next one shows up, so read each new message.

title: Full volume, stale pidfile
story: app-writer died when its log volume filled up. Restarting it with start-writer prints "already running", yet nothing is running. The log volume /var/log/app is also nearly full. Several things are wrong at once. Fixing the first one will not be enough.
goals: app-writer is running and writes to /var/log/app/heartbeat.log.
/var/log/app is under 50 percent full.
hints: df -h /var/log/app and ls -lh /var/log/app show what fills the volume.
start-writer trusts /run/app-writer.pid. Does the process with that PID exist? ps | grep app-writer
Free the space (the big file dump.tmp is safe to remove), delete the stale pidfile, then run start-writer.
solution:
df -h /var/log/app
ls -lh /var/log/app
rm /var/log/app/dump.tmp
rm /run/app-writer.pid
start-writer

why.q: Why do two small faults look like one big failure?
o: One fault always causes the other
Each one alone would stop the service
why.x: A full disk and a stale pidfile both block the start. Fixing only one leaves it down.

title: Uploads fail for three reasons
story: Users cannot upload files. The upload helper store-upload runs as the user www and reports a different error each time it is run. The directory it should write to is /srv/uploads/incoming. Several things are wrong at once. Fixing the first one will not be enough.
goals: As the user www, store-upload creates a file in /srv/uploads/incoming and prints OK.
hints: Test it as the service does: su -s /bin/sh www -c store-upload
Read the message. Then check the path in /etc/uploader.conf, who owns /srv/uploads/incoming, and whether www can enter /srv (ls -ld /srv).
Fix each in turn: the path in the config, chown www /srv/uploads/incoming, chmod 755 /srv.
solution:
su -s /bin/sh www -c store-upload
sed -i "s#/srv/upload\$#/srv/uploads/incoming#" /etc/uploader.conf
chmod 755 /srv
chown www /srv/uploads/incoming
su -s /bin/sh www -c store-upload

why.q: What must be true for a user to write into /srv/uploads/incoming?
o: Every folder in the path is enterable and the last one is writable
why.x: Path access needs x on every parent folder and w on the target folder, for the right user.

title: No route, and the router does not forward
story: The orders app cannot reach the database at 10.0.2.10. A new router sits between them at 10.0.1.254. Nobody added a route on this host, and the router was never told to forward packets. Several things are wrong at once. Fixing the first one will not be enough. Inside the machine: inns NAME command runs a command inside a private network (ls /run/ns).
goals: wget http://10.0.2.10:5432/ answers "orders-db ready".
A route to 10.0.2.0/24 exists on this host and the router forwards packets.
hints: ping -c1 10.0.1.254 works, ping -c1 -W1 10.0.2.10 does not. Start with the route: ip route add 10.0.2.0/24 via 10.0.1.254
It still fails. Look inside the router: inns router cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward
Turn forwarding on: inns router sh -c "echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward"
solution:
ip route add 10.0.2.0/24 via 10.0.1.254
inns router sh -c "echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward"
wget -qO- http://10.0.2.10:5432/

why.q: Why was one fix not enough?
o: The host needed a route and the router needed forwarding
why.x: A packet needs a way out (route) and a router willing to pass it (forwarding).

title: A new service with three problems
story: The reports service was installed from a ticket. It will not start; every fix reveals the next problem. Get it running, with its settings, and make sure it comes back after a reboot. This lab uses a small imitation of systemctl. Several things are wrong at once. Fixing the first one will not be enough.
goals: reports is active and /run/reports.dir says /var/reports.
reports is enabled.
hints: systemctl status reports and journalctl -u reports -n 10 name the current problem. Fix it, run systemctl daemon-reload, start again, read the next message.
The first problem is the path of the program (find /opt/reports -type f). The second is the environment file (find /etc/reports -type f).
The third has nothing to do with starting: systemctl is-enabled reports. Use systemctl enable reports.
solution:
journalctl -u reports -n 5
sed -i "s#/opt/reports/reportd#/opt/reports/bin/reportd#" /etc/systemd/system/reports.service
sed -i "s#/etc/reports.env#/etc/reports/reports.env#" /etc/systemd/system/reports.service
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable --now reports

why.q: Why does it help to read journalctl after every fix?
o: Each failure message names the next problem
why.x: The journal shows what the service manager saw. When one error goes, the next appears there.

title: The cleanup job that never runs
story: The cleanup script should run every five minutes and write /run/clean.done. It has never run. Nobody noticed, because nothing complains. Several things are wrong at once. Fixing the first one will not be enough.
goals: crond is running.
The crontab line uses the full path of the script, and the script is executable and works with the minimal environment cron gives it.
hints: ps | grep crond: is the scheduler running at all? crontab -l shows the job.
Cron runs jobs with a tiny PATH, so a bare script name is not found. Use the full path /usr/local/bin/nightly-clean.sh. Also check ls -l on the script.
Start the scheduler with crond -b. Replace the crontab: echo "*/5 * * * * /usr/local/bin/nightly-clean.sh" | crontab -
solution:
ps | grep crond
crontab -l
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/nightly-clean.sh
echo "*/5 * * * * /usr/local/bin/nightly-clean.sh" | crontab -
crond -b

why.q: Why must cron jobs use absolute paths?
o: Cron runs with almost no PATH
why.x: Cron does not read your profile. A bare script name is often not found.

title: The backup script that quietly does nothing
story: The site backup has not produced an archive for two weeks. The script /usr/local/bin/backup-site.sh is run from cron, which hides its errors. It needs to create /backup/daily/site-*.tar.gz that contains index.html. Several things are wrong at once. Fixing the first one will not be enough.
goals: The script is executable.
Running it produces /backup/daily/site-*.tar.gz that contains index.html.
hints: Run it by hand and read the errors: /usr/local/bin/backup-site.sh
Permissions first (ls -l). Then the source directory (it has a typo: ls /srv) and the destination (does /backup/daily exist?).
chmod +x the script, fix SRC with sed, and mkdir -p /backup/daily.
solution:
/usr/local/bin/backup-site.sh
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/backup-site.sh
sed -i "s#/srv/sitee#/srv/site#" /usr/local/bin/backup-site.sh
mkdir -p /backup/daily
/usr/local/bin/backup-site.sh
ls /backup/daily

why.q: Why test the backup by running it with env -i?
o: It shows what the script does with an empty environment, like cron
why.x: env -i removes variables like PATH. If it works there, it works from cron.

title: Port taken, and the wrong database
story: The new web v2 must listen on port 8080 and use the database db.internal. start-web fails. Behind the failure there are two separate problems, and fixing only one leaves the site broken. Several things are wrong at once. Fixing the first one will not be enough.
goals: http://127.0.0.1:8080/ answers "web v2".
/run/web.status says db=db.internal.
hints: Run start-web and read the error. netstat -tln shows who holds 8080; ps shows the old server.
Stop the old server (kill $(pidof httpd)). Then look at /etc/web.env: the database name is the old one.
Edit APP_DB in /etc/web.env, then run start-web again and check /run/web.status.
solution:
start-web
netstat -tln
kill $(pidof httpd)
sed -i "s/db.old/db.internal/" /etc/web.env
start-web
wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/

why.q: Why check the running service after you start it?
o: The service reports errors by itself
A started process can still use wrong settings
why.x: Only reading the result (status file, response) shows it uses the intended database and port.

title: Rotated, but the app still writes to the old file
story: Log rotation ran last night. Since then app.log is empty, the app seems silent, and the log volume is nearly full of old rotations. The logger is app-logger. Several things are wrong at once. Fixing the first one will not be enough.
goals: New lines appear in /var/log/app/app.log.
The log volume /var/log/app is under 70 percent full.
hints: ls -l /var/log/app: which file keeps growing? A process keeps writing to the file it opened, even after it was renamed.
The logger re-opens its log when it gets the HUP signal: kill -HUP $(pidof app-logger)
Free space: the old rotations app.log.2 and app.log.3 can be removed (or gzip them).
solution:
ls -lh /var/log/app
kill -HUP $(pidof app-logger)
rm /var/log/app/app.log.2 /var/log/app/app.log.3
df -h /var/log/app
tail /var/log/app/app.log

why.q: Why did the app keep writing to the rotated file?
o: It holds the open file, not the name
why.x: After mv, the app's file handle still points to the moved file. A reopen signal (HUP) switches it to the new one.

title: The service three people broke
story: ghost-app must run as the user ghost and listen on port 8088. start-ghost refuses to start, and each time you fix its complaint, it finds another. Previous owners left a mess. Several things are wrong at once. Fixing the first one will not be enough.
goals: ghost-app runs as the user ghost (uid 1200).
/var/lib/ghost/state says ok port=8088.
hints: Run start-ghost and read what it says. The first message is about a lock file in /run.
Next: the config /etc/ghost.conf. cat -A shows hidden characters; a ^M at the end of a line is a Windows line ending. Remove it with sed -i "s/\r$//".
Last: the data folder /var/lib/ghost must belong to the user ghost: chown ghost /var/lib/ghost
solution:
start-ghost
rm /run/ghost.lock
sed -i "s/\r$//" /etc/ghost.conf
chown ghost /var/lib/ghost
start-ghost
cat /var/lib/ghost/state

why.q: Why is a service sometimes blocked by a lock file?
o: A previous run left it behind and the new run refuses to start
why.x: A lock file stops two copies at once. After a crash it stays, so check that no process holds it before removing.

title: The service that will not start because of its key
story: After a handover, shop-tls will not start. The error mentions the private key. Nobody changed the certificate. Fix the problem and start the service. The key must stay where it is. A small web service listens on 127.0.0.1:8443 with TLS (start, stop and restart it with shop-tls; its settings are in /etc/shop-tls.conf; certificates are in /etc/tls). Test it like a client would: openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -verify_hostname shop.lab -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.pem -brief < /dev/null
goals: The service is running and the client check passes.
The private key is readable only by its owner.
hints: Run shop-tls start and read the message. It names the key file and says who can read it.
ls -l /etc/tls/shop.key shows the permissions. A private key must not be readable by the group or by others.
chmod 600 /etc/tls/shop.key, then shop-tls start.
solution:
shop-tls start
ls -l /etc/tls/shop.key
chmod 600 /etc/tls/shop.key
shop-tls start
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.pem -brief < /dev/null

why.q: Why is a private key kept at mode 600?
o: So the service can write to it
Anyone who can read the key can impersonate the server
Because TLS needs the file to be hidden from the certificate
So the key cannot be copied by the owner
why.x: The private key is what proves the server is the one named in the certificate. If other users can read it, they can copy it and impersonate the server. Many services refuse to start with a loose key for this reason.

title: The client does not trust the company CA
story: The checkout client calls the shop over TLS and fails: "unable to get local issuer certificate". The service itself is fine; its certificate is signed by the company's own CA. The CA certificate is in /root/lab-root-ca.pem. Make this machine trust it the standard way. A small web service listens on 127.0.0.1:8443 with TLS (start, stop and restart it with shop-tls; its settings are in /etc/shop-tls.conf; certificates are in /etc/tls). Test it like a client would: openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -verify_hostname shop.lab -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.pem -brief < /dev/null
goals: openssl s_client (the command in the story) prints "Verification: OK".
The company CA is in the system trust bundle, added the way Debian does it.
hints: Run the s_client command. The Verification line says the issuer is not known to this machine.
The system bundle is /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.pem. It is rebuilt by update-ca-certificates from files ending in .crt in /usr/local/share/ca-certificates.
cp /root/lab-root-ca.pem /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/lab-root-ca.crt, then update-ca-certificates. The file name must end in .crt.
solution:
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.pem -brief < /dev/null
cp /root/lab-root-ca.pem /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/lab-root-ca.crt
update-ca-certificates
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -verify_hostname shop.lab -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.pem -brief < /dev/null

why.q: Why does a certificate signed by your own CA fail on a fresh machine?
o: The certificate is expired by default
The machine only trusts the roots in its bundle, and your CA is not one of them
The server must send its private key
why.x: A client trusts a certificate only if it chains to a root in its own trust store. A company CA is not in the default store, so you add it deliberately, on every machine that should trust it.

title: The certificate that expired in the spring
story: Customers report certificate errors on the shop. The service has run for years without changes. Renew the certificate from the existing request (/etc/tls/shop.csr) with the issuing CA on this machine (/etc/tls/inter.pem and inter.key), for 90 days, and reload the service. A small web service listens on 127.0.0.1:8443 with TLS (start, stop and restart it with shop-tls; its settings are in /etc/shop-tls.conf; certificates are in /etc/tls). Test it like a client would: openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -verify_hostname shop.lab -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.pem -brief < /dev/null
goals: openssl s_client (the command in the story) prints "Verification: OK".
The new certificate is valid now and the service serves it.
hints: Run the s_client command and read the Verification error. Then: openssl x509 -in /etc/tls/shop.pem -noout -dates
Sign the existing request again: openssl x509 -req -in /etc/tls/shop.csr -CA /etc/tls/inter.pem -CAkey /etc/tls/inter.key -CAcreateserial -days 90 -copy_extensions copy -out /etc/tls/shop.pem
A running service keeps the old certificate in memory. shop-tls restart loads the new file.
solution:
openssl x509 -in /etc/tls/shop.pem -noout -dates
openssl x509 -req -in /etc/tls/shop.csr -CA /etc/tls/inter.pem -CAkey /etc/tls/inter.key -CAcreateserial -days 90 -copy_extensions copy -out /etc/tls/shop.pem
shop-tls restart

why.q: Why was a restart needed after replacing the certificate file?
o: The file is only read when the service starts
Restarting makes the certificate longer lived
The CA refuses to sign while the service runs
why.x: This service reads its certificate once at start-up. Replacing the file changes nothing for new connections until the service reloads it. Many servers can reload without a full restart; this one cannot.

title: A valid certificate for the wrong name
story: The shop certificate is signed by the right CA and has not expired, yet the client says the name does not match. The shop is reached as shop.lab. Issue a new certificate from /etc/tls/shop.csr that names shop.lab (and keep www.shop.lab too), using the issuing CA on this machine. A small web service listens on 127.0.0.1:8443 with TLS (start, stop and restart it with shop-tls; its settings are in /etc/shop-tls.conf; certificates are in /etc/tls). Test it like a client would: openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -verify_hostname shop.lab -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.pem -brief < /dev/null
goals: openssl s_client (the command in the story) prints "Verification: OK".
The certificate names shop.lab and www.shop.lab.
hints: Read the Verification line: it is about the hostname, not the CA.
openssl x509 -in /etc/tls/shop.pem -noout -ext subjectAltName shows the names the certificate covers. Clients check this list, not the common name.
Write an extension file: printf 'subjectAltName=DNS:shop.lab,DNS:www.shop.lab\n' > /tmp/san.cnf. Then sign again with -extfile /tmp/san.cnf, and shop-tls restart.
solution:
openssl x509 -in /etc/tls/shop.pem -noout -ext subjectAltName
printf 'subjectAltName=DNS:shop.lab,DNS:www.shop.lab\n' > /tmp/san.cnf
openssl x509 -req -in /etc/tls/shop.csr -CA /etc/tls/inter.pem -CAkey /etc/tls/inter.key -CAcreateserial -days 90 -extfile /tmp/san.cnf -out /etc/tls/shop.pem
shop-tls restart

why.q: Which part of a certificate do modern clients use to match the hostname?
why.x: Modern clients match the name against the subject alternative names (SAN) list. The common name is ignored when SANs exist, so a certificate must list every name it should serve.

title: The chain that stops short
story: Browsers open the shop, but a script on a server says "unable to verify the first certificate" / "unable to get local issuer certificate". The root CA is trusted on this machine. The shop certificate is signed by an intermediate CA (/etc/tls/inter.pem), not by the root. Fix what the service sends, without changing the trust bundle. A small web service listens on 127.0.0.1:8443 with TLS (start, stop and restart it with shop-tls; its settings are in /etc/shop-tls.conf; certificates are in /etc/tls). Test it like a client would: openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -verify_hostname shop.lab -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.pem -brief < /dev/null
goals: openssl s_client (the command in the story) prints "Verification: OK".
The service sends the intermediate certificate with its own.
hints: Run: openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -showcerts < /dev/null  and count the certificates the server sends.
The root is trusted, the shop certificate is signed by the intermediate, and the server did not send the intermediate. Browsers can fetch it themselves; scripts cannot.
The service reads extra chain certificates from CHAIN in /etc/shop-tls.conf (/etc/tls/chain.pem), and it is empty. Put the intermediate in it and restart.
solution:
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -showcerts < /dev/null | grep -c BEGIN
cp /etc/tls/inter.pem /etc/tls/chain.pem
shop-tls restart

why.q: Why do browsers cope with a missing intermediate when scripts do not?
o: Browsers can fetch or remember missing intermediates; most command-line clients do not
why.x: Browsers cache intermediates and can download them from the certificate's issuer link. Most command-line clients only use what the server sends, so the server must send the full chain except the root.

title: The key that belongs to the old certificate
story: The shop certificate was renewed yesterday and the service was stopped for the change. Now shop-tls will not start and complains about the key. The old key is still in /etc/tls (shop-old.key); the new one is shop.key. Find the cause and start the service, changing as little as possible. A small web service listens on 127.0.0.1:8443 with TLS (start, stop and restart it with shop-tls; its settings are in /etc/shop-tls.conf; certificates are in /etc/tls). Test it like a client would: openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -verify_hostname shop.lab -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.pem -brief < /dev/null
goals: openssl s_client (the command in the story) prints "Verification: OK".
The service uses the key that matches the certificate.
hints: Run shop-tls start and read the error: "key values mismatch".
Compare the public key in the certificate with the one derived from each key: openssl x509 -in /etc/tls/shop.pem -noout -pubkey | md5sum  and  openssl pkey -in /etc/tls/shop.key -pubout | md5sum
Only one key matches. /etc/shop-tls.conf points KEY at the wrong file: sed -i or edit it, then shop-tls start.
solution:
shop-tls start
openssl x509 -in /etc/tls/shop.pem -noout -pubkey | md5sum
openssl pkey -in /etc/tls/shop.key -pubout | md5sum
openssl pkey -in /etc/tls/shop-old.key -pubout | md5sum
sed -i "s#shop-old.key#shop.key#" /etc/shop-tls.conf
shop-tls start

why.q: How can you tell whether a private key matches a certificate?
o: Compare the public key inside the certificate with the public key derived from the private key
Check that both files have the same size
Check that the key is newer than the certificate
why.x: A certificate contains the public half of a key pair. Deriving the public key from a private key and comparing it with the certificate's shows whether they are a pair, whatever the files are called.

title: The gateway that only speaks TLS 1.3
story: The payment gateway connects to the shop and fails the handshake with "protocol version". Its policy allows TLS 1.3 only. The shop service was pinned to TLS 1.2 years ago, and a few old internal clients still need 1.2, so they must keep working. Fix the service, not the gateway. A small web service listens on 127.0.0.1:8443 with TLS (start, stop and restart it with shop-tls; its settings are in /etc/shop-tls.conf; certificates are in /etc/tls). Test it like a client would: openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -verify_hostname shop.lab -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.pem -brief < /dev/null
goals: The gateway check (openssl s_client -tls1_3 ...) passes: "Verification: OK".
A client limited to TLS 1.2 still connects.
hints: Try the gateway check: add -tls1_3 to the s_client command. Then look at /etc/shop-tls.conf: the PROTOCOLS line.
PROTOCOLS=tls1_2 pins the service to TLS 1.2 (it becomes the -tls1_2 option). Pinning to 1.3 instead would break the old clients.
Leave PROTOCOLS empty so the service offers both, then shop-tls restart. Test both with -tls1_3 and -tls1_2.
solution:
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 -servername shop.lab -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-bundle.pem -tls1_3 -brief < /dev/null
cat /etc/shop-tls.conf
sed -i "s/^PROTOCOLS=.*/PROTOCOLS=/" /etc/shop-tls.conf
shop-tls restart

why.q: Why not pin the service to TLS 1.3 only?
o: Older clients that only speak 1.2 would stop working
why.x: Offering both versions lets each client use the best one it supports. Pinning to 1.3 would lock out every client that cannot speak it. Raising the minimum is a deliberate step taken once the old clients are gone.

title: Which certificate expires first?
story: Three internal sites keep their certificates in /etc/tls/sites: site-alpha.pem, site-beta.pem and site-gamma.pem. An audit wants to know which one needs renewal first. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.

Compare the years first, then the months and days.
solution:
for f in /etc/tls/sites/*.pem; do echo $f $(openssl x509 -noout -enddate -in $f); done
Answer: beta
ask: Which site (alpha, beta or gamma) has the certificate that expires first?

title: Who signed the shop certificate?
story: A service answers on 127.0.0.1:8443 with TLS. Before trusting it, the security team wants to know which CA signed the certificate it presents. Diagnose only: find the cause, do not fix it.
goals: Look around the machine with real commands. Do not change anything. Type your diagnosis in the box under the terminal and press Submit.

title: The dependency that is too old
story: apt install report-tool fails: it needs libchart 2.0 or newer, but the repository only has 1.4. libchart is at 2.0 or newer.

title: The lock that someone is holding
story: apt install jq-lite stops with "Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend. It is held by process ...". Nothing else seems to be installing anything. The process that held the lock is no longer running.
hints: The error names the process and its program. Look at it: ps | grep unattended

unattended-upgrade is meant to finish in minutes. This one has been running since boot and is stuck. Deleting the lock file would let two package tools run at once, which can corrupt the package database.
Stop the stuck process: kill $(cat /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend). Then apt install -y jq-lite.
solution:

apt install -y jq-lite

why.q: Why is deleting the lock file the wrong fix?
o: The file is needed to install packages
It lets two package tools change the database at once, which can corrupt it
The lock file is recreated anyway
why.x: The lock exists to stop two tools editing the package database together. If another process really holds it, removing the file hides the problem and risks a corrupt database. Find the holder, wait for it or stop it, then continue.

title: The download that does not match
story: apt install payd-lite downloads the package and fails with "Hash Sum mismatch".
